Golden Gh0st RAT credential collection from 360 / QQ / Skype browser stores AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a non-browser process reading credential and cookie databases inside 360 Secure Browser, 360 Speed Browser, Tencent QQ Browser, Skype, Chrome, or Firefox profiles - the exact application set Golden Gh0st RAT targets for data theft. Rationale: Directly targets the article's named collection victims - 360 Secure Browser, 360 Speed Browser, QQ Browser, Skype, Chrome, Firefox - by watching for a NON-browser process touching their secret stores (Login Data/key4.db/Cookies). The 360/QQ browser set is highly specific to Chinese-cybercrime tooling and rare outside APAC targeting. Datadog left empty: Sysmon does not emit reliable file-read telemetry for this access pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/goldeneyedog-subgroup-linked-to.html • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/roningloader
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup/sync agent (OneDrive, Veeam, browser-profile backup) reading profile folders
  • Password-manager import utility legitimately parsing browser Login Data
  • Enterprise DLP/AV engine scanning browser profile directories
  • Browser-migration tool copying profiles between installs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("onedrive.exe","veeam.agent.exe","backup.exe","msmpeng.exe","dlpsensor.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName and its path - an unsigned binary in Temp/AppData or a system binary (regsvr32/rundll32) reading key4.db is high-confidence; a known backup agent is likely benign. 2. Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and force-reset the browser-stored credentials for the affected user (email, SSO, VPN, financial). 3. Hunt: correlate to the regsvr32/TrustedInstaller C2 beacon and campaign hashes on the same host, and check for SOCKS-proxy / screenshot / keylog artifacts consistent with Golden Gh0st RAT.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\360se6\", @"\360Chrome\", @"\360ChromeX\", @"\Tencent\QQBrowser\", @"\Skype\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\", @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","logins.json","key4.db","cookies.sqlite","History")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","firefox.exe","360se.exe","360chrome.exe","qqbrowser.exe","msedge.exe","skype.exe","explorer.exe","searchprotocolhost.exe","msmpeng.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\360se6\", @"\360Chrome\", @"\360ChromeX\", @"\Tencent\QQBrowser\", @"\Skype\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\", @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","logins.json","key4.db","cookies.sqlite","History")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","firefox.exe","360se.exe","360chrome.exe","qqbrowser.exe","msedge.exe","skype.exe","explorer.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    from datamodel=Web

| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

SecurityEvent

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'

falsepositives:

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Inside the Search for "Clean" Residential Proxies for Carding

BleepingComputer
2026-07-17 3 use cases 0 techniques 1 kill-chain phase detected

Residential proxies are no longer the silver bullet they once were for carding. Flare explains why cybercriminals increasingly seek "clean" residential proxies and combine them with browser fingerprints, device profiles, and other identity signals to evade modern fraud detection. [...]

Domainsnetnut.com netnut.io alarum.io ascarding.net

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Corporate endpoint browsing the ascarding.net carding forum · [LLM] Internal host connecting to NetNut / Alarum residential-proxy infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Corporate endpoint browsing the ascarding.net carding forum AICommand & Control High
Hunts internal hosts resolving or connecting to ascarding.net ("The Carding Forum Asylum"), the forum hosting the 'Getting the Cleanest Possible IPs for Carding' guide central to this Flare report. Near-zero legitimate business reason for a corporate device to reach a carding marketplace, making it a high-fidelity insider-fraud / compromised-host signal. Rationale: Uses the exact carding-forum domain ascarding.net named/screenshotted in the article and confirmed via search as 'The Carding Forum Asylum' hosting the cited carding guide; corporate endpoints have virtually no legitimate reason to reach it, so it is high-fidelity with minimal enumeration. Cross-checked against: • https://ascarding.net/threads/3970/ • https://ascarding.net/forums/44/
ATT&CKT1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intelligence analyst manually browsing the forum from a sanctioned research workstation
  • SOC analyst validating an IOC during triage
  • Malware sandbox / detonation VM following a URL from a feed
  • Security-vendor crawler running on corporate egress
  • User clicking an ascarding.net link embedded in a phishing/threat-report email
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in~ ("ti-research-vm01","soc-sandbox01") or InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-tithreatintel"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the device, user and initiating process (browser vs. non-browser/automation). Confirm the host is not a sanctioned TI/research asset and the account is not a security analyst. 2) Contain: if the device is a standard corporate endpoint, isolate it, force credential reset for the user, and block ascarding.net at the proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for connections to netnut.com/netnut.io/alarum.io and other proxy vendors, antidetect-browser installs (e.g. Dolphin, GoLogin, Multilogin), and any access to internal payment/finance systems in the surrounding window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "ascarding.net"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "ascarding.net"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Endpoint DNS/Web Access to ascarding.net Carding Forum
id: 6f3b9a12-4c2e-4d7a-9f11-2a7c8e6b1d04
description: Detects a host resolving or connecting to ascarding.net, a known carding forum central to the Flare residential-proxy carding report.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/inside-the-search-for-clean-residential-proxies-for-carding/
  - https://ascarding.net/threads/3970/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/17
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    query|contains: 'ascarding.net'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(*ascarding.net* OR *ASCARDING.NET*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/ascarding\.net/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_host="*ascarding.net*" OR All_Traffic.url="*ascarding.net*" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_host="*ascarding.net*" OR All_Traffic.url="*ascarding.net*" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Internal host connecting to NetNut / Alarum residential-proxy infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts corporate devices resolving or connecting to netnut.com, netnut.io or alarum.io — the residential-proxy vendor (Alarum Technologies / NetNut) whose exit nodes the FBI seized in July 2026 and which carders in this report seek for 'clean' finance-compatible IPs. A device reaching these gateways typically indicates residential-proxy client software running locally to anonymize/geo-shift outbound sessions. Rationale: Uses the four concrete vendor domains named in the article (netnut.com, netnut.io, alarum.io) corroborated by the FBI/Google NetNut-Popa seizure; DNS to these gateways from an endpoint is a strong indicator of residential-proxy client tooling rather than incidental browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/07/fbi-seizes-netnut-proxy-platform-popa-botnet/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/fbi-google-take-down-netnut-proxy/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/netnut-proxy-network-disrupted-2-million-infected-devices-cut-off/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1090.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing / ad-verification team legitimately licensing NetNut for localized ad checks
  • Brand-protection or SEO tooling using residential proxies for geo testing
  • QA/localization team validating region-specific site rendering
  • Threat-intel analyst visiting the vendor site post-seizure to review the takedown
  • Security researcher enumerating proxy vendors from a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName startswith "mktg-" or InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-adverify","svc-brandprotect"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine which process reached the domain (a browser tab to the marketing site is far lower risk than a headless/service binary hitting a gateway API). Check whether the user/device belongs to a sanctioned marketing or research function. 2) Contain: for non-sanctioned hosts, isolate the endpoint, hunt for and remove residential-proxy client binaries, and block netnut.com/netnut.io/alarum.io at DNS/proxy. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host/user with ascarding.net access, antidetect-browser artefacts, and abnormal logins to internal finance/payment portals or customer PII stores in the surrounding window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("netnut.com","netnut.io","alarum.io")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by FirstSeen desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("netnut.com","netnut.io","alarum.io")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by FirstSeen desc

author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:

detection:

level: medium

#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(netnut\.(com|io)|alarum\.io)/i

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_host IN ("*netnut.com","*netnut.io","*alarum.io") OR All_Traffic.url IN ("*netnut.com*","*netnut.io*","*alarum.io*")) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("netnut.com", "netnut.io", "alarum.io", "ascarding.net")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["netnut.com", "netnut.io", "alarum.io", "ascarding.net"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake Coding Tests Deliver OtterCookie-Aligned Malware Hidden in SVG Flag Images
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] serverValidation.js loader executed by Node from trojanized coding-test repo
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Node.js runtime beaconing to REF9403 rightwidth.dev Socket.IO C2 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OtterCookie file stealer reading AI coding-assistant config dirs (.claude/.cursor/.windsurf) · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Node.js runtime beaconing to REF9403 rightwidth.dev Socket.IO C2 AICommand & Control High
Hunts a node.exe/npm process resolving or connecting to the REF9403 command-and-control infrastructure (ldb/upload/controller.rightwidth.dev) used by the OtterCookie-aligned four-stage payload. Node is not a browser, so an interpreter reaching this dev-TLD domain family is a high-fidelity C2 signal specific to the fake-coding-test lure. Rationale: Anchors on the four confirmed C2 subdomains (ldb/upload/controller.rightwidth.dev) plus a node/npm initiator so it fires on interpreter-driven C2 even though the domain is single-sourced to Elastic; a JS runtime resolving a dev-TLD attacker domain is near-zero in benign traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/beavertail-and-ottercookie/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/11/contagious-interview-malware-delivered-through-fake-developer-job-interviews/ • https://cyberandramen.net/2026/04/04/ottercookie-expands-targeting-to-ai-coding-tools-analysis-of-a-trojanized-npm-campaign/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using a package or SaaS hosted on a *.rightwidth.dev subdomain (validate the specific FQDN against the IOC list)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned analysis VM
  • Corporate proxy/DNS-sinkhole re-resolving the domain for blocking (resolver IP, not endpoint)
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment tooling actively resolving IOCs
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl == "rightwidth.dev" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("threatintel","ioc-check","sandbox"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving process is node/npm and pull InitiatingProcessCommandLine to find the trojanized repo path; check whether the host cloned a repo referencing Next.js v14/NestJS/Auth.js lure stack. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block *.rightwidth.dev at DNS/proxy, and kill the node process tree; preserve the repo and node_modules for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same aid/DeviceName for reads of .claude/.cursor/.windsurf dirs, browser Login Data, and crypto-wallet extension storage, and rotate any credentials/AI-service tokens present on the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "rightwidth.dev" or RemoteUrl in~ ("ldb.rightwidth.dev","upload.rightwidth.dev","controller.rightwidth.dev","rightwidth.dev")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.cmd","npm","yarn.cmd","electron.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery endswith "rightwidth.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OtterCookie file stealer reading AI coding-assistant config dirs (.claude/.cursor/.windsurf) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a Node.js process enumerating the AI coding-tool configuration directories (.claude, .cursor, .gemini, .windsurf, .pearai, .llama) that OtterCookie's file-stealer module explicitly harvests for API keys, tokens and LLM conversation logs. This directory set touched by a JS interpreter is the novel differentiator in the REF9403 campaign. Rationale: Uses the exact six AI-tool config dir names OtterCookie enumerates (corroborated by Talos and cyberandramen.net) with a node.exe initiator; a JS runtime crawling .claude/.cursor/.windsurf together is behaviour no legitimate build tool exhibits. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberandramen.net/2026/04/04/ottercookie-expands-targeting-to-ai-coding-tools-analysis-of-a-trojanized-npm-campaign/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/beavertail-and-ottercookie/
ATT&CKT1005 T1552.001 T1119
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The AI tools themselves updating their config (initiating process is cursor.exe/claude.exe, not node.exe)
  • A developer's own dotfile-sync or backup script running under node reading these dirs
  • VS Code extensions built on Node performing legitimate config reads of a single tool
  • Security tooling inventorying installed AI extensions
Suppression filter
| where DirsTouched >= 2 and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "dotfiles-sync"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect InitiatingProcessCommandLine — legitimate access reads one tool dir; OtterCookie sweeps all six plus .env/.pem/.key/.ssh. Confirm the parent is an npm-launched project, not the AI IDE. 2) Contain: isolate host, suspend the node process, and immediately rotate all AI-service API tokens (Claude/Cursor/Gemini) and any secrets found in the swept directories. 3) Hunt: correlate with rightwidth.dev C2 (UC1) and serverValidation.js execution (UC3) on the same host, and check for browser Login Data / crypto-wallet extension reads.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\.claude\\","\\.cursor\\","\\.gemini\\","\\.windsurf\\","\\.pearai\\","\\.llama\\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FileCount=dcount(FileName), DirsTouched=make_set(FolderPath, 10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\.claude\\","\\.cursor\\","\\.gemini\\","\\.windsurf\\","\\.pearai\\","\\.llama\\")
| summarize FileCount=dcount(TargetFilePath), Dirs=make_set(TargetFilePath, 10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Node.js Process Accessing AI Coding-Assistant Config Directories (OtterCookie)

#event_simpleName=/^(FileOpenInfo|FileWritten)$/ ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm)\.exe$/i | TargetFileName=/\\\.(claude|cursor|gemini|windsurf|pearai|llama)\\/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true))

serverValidation.js loader executed by Node from trojanized coding-test repo AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the OtterCookie loader serverValidation.js, which reassembles the base64 payload fragments hidden in HTML comments across the country-flag SVG images (AE.svg, AF.svg) in the repo's assets directory. Detection targets the named loader script running under node as part of the fake coding-assessment repo. Rationale: Uses the exact loader filename serverValidation.js named by Elastic plus a node interpreter; dual proc+filewrite Defender coverage catches both cmdline-visible and require()-loaded execution, so the detection survives whether the script is passed as an arg or imported. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/north-korea-linked-hackers-hide.html • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/beavertail-and-ottercookie/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027.003 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate project genuinely shipping an unrelated file named serverValidation.js (verify repo origin and whether it reads SVG assets)
  • Developer authoring server-side validation logic in a file coincidentally named the same
  • CI/CD pipeline running a benign validation step under node
Response runbook
1) Triage: locate the parent repo dir, inspect the assets/ folder for country-flag SVGs (AE.svg, AF.svg) containing base64 in HTML comments, and read serverValidation.js for base64 reassembly/eval logic. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the node tree, quarantine the repo, and block rightwidth.dev. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same repo/loader across other developer endpoints (Slack-lure victims), and pivot to UC1 C2 beacons and UC2 AI-config-dir reads; rotate credentials on any confirmed host.
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node") and ProcessCommandLine has "serverValidation.js"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="proc", InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "serverValidation.js"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="filewrite", InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath )
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "serverValidation.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High

DeviceProcessEvents

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-07-17 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A technical analysis of three chained zero-day vulnerabilities in Siemens ROX II OT switches that allow privilege escalation and persistent root access. The post Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II xz-as-cat arbitrary disclosure of shadow/private keys (CVE-2025-40948) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II feature-key gpgv command injection to root (CVE-2025-40947) · [LLM] Siemens ROX II three-stage zero-day chain temporal correlation (CVE-2025-40948/40947/40949) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II root cron persistence via web task scheduler (CVE-2025-40949) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Siemens ROX II xz-as-cat arbitrary disclosure of shadow/private keys (CVE-2025-40948) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the CVE-2025-40948 stage where a root-privileged xz utility is misused with decompress-to-stdout flags to read sensitive files (/etc/shadow, SSH/TLS private keys, config) on a Ruggedcom ROX II OT switch. Article-specific: xz functioning like cat against credential-bearing files is the reconnaissance foothold of the chain. Rationale: Uses the article's exact CVE-2025-40948 mechanic — root-privileged xz used like cat (decompress-to-stdout) against password hashes and private keys. Pairing xz with a sensitive-file target and a stdout/decompress flag makes it high-fidelity; xz legitimately never streams /etc/shadow. Cross-checked NVD and CISA ICSA-26-134-02. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02 • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/siemens-rox-ii-zero-day-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1003.008 T1552.004 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin decompressing a .xz log/backup archive with xz -dc to a pager
  • Firmware/update tooling that pipes xz -d output during a package install
  • A monitoring script that reads a config file that happens to end in .key but is not a private key
  • Backup jobs streaming compressed archives from /etc via xz
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("backup","firmware","/var/log/") and not SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/shadow","id_rsa","id_dsa","ssl/private"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full Syslog/auditd EXECVE line — confirm the xz target is /etc/shadow, an SSH/TLS private key, or a credential config, and identify the invoking user/session on the ROX II switch. 2) Contain: isolate the switch's management plane (block untrusted access to the web/CLI mgmt VLAN), rotate any exposed device keys/passwords, and confirm firmware is upgraded to V2.17.1. 3) Hunt: on the same device look for the follow-on chain — feature-key command injection (CVE-2025-40947) and root crontab modification (CVE-2025-40949) within the following minutes.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has "xz" or SyslogMessage has "xz"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/shadow","id_rsa","id_dsa","ssl/private",".pem",".key")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("--decompress","-dc"," -d ","--stdout","-c ")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage, Facility, SeverityLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Siemens ROX II xz Misused to Read Sensitive Files (CVE-2025-40948)
id: 5b1f4d2e-7a3c-4e9b-9c21-8f0a1d6b3e77
description: Detects the xz utility invoked with decompress-to-stdout flags against credential-bearing files, the arbitrary file disclosure stage of the Siemens Ruggedcom ROX II exploit chain.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/siemens-rox-ii-zero-day-vulnerabilities/
  - https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02

source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:xz @process.command_line:(*shadow* OR *id_rsa* OR *id_dsa* OR *.key OR *ssl/private* OR *.pem*)

Siemens ROX II feature-key gpgv command injection to root (CVE-2025-40947) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts CVE-2025-40947: an attacker-controlled feature-key payload submitted to the ROX II web/CLI management is inserted unsanitized into a root-privileged command, allowing shell command injection. Article-specific: feature-key validation input carrying shell metacharacters is the privilege-escalation pivot of the chain. Rationale: Grounded in the CVE-2025-40947 description — an unsanitized feature-key payload inserted directly into a root command. Detecting shell metacharacters (;, |, &&, $(), backtick, $IFS) inside a feature-key request/log line is high-fidelity because a legitimate feature key is an opaque signed token with no shell syntax. Corroborated via NVD and CISA ICSA-26-134-02. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin pasting a legitimate feature key that coincidentally contains a semicolon-delimited field
  • WAF/proxy URL-decoding artifacts that surface encoded characters in benign query strings
  • Automated inventory tooling querying the feature-key endpoint without injection payloads
  • Penetration-test / vulnerability-scanner traffic fuzzing the mgmt interface
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("scanner","nessus","qualys") or ProcessName has_any ("nessus","scan"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: reconstruct the feature-key request/log entry — confirm shell metacharacters are inside the attacker-controlled key field rather than a benign token, and identify the authenticated user and source IP. 2) Contain: revoke the session, restrict the ROX II management interface to a trusted jump host, and verify firmware V2.17.1 is applied (the fix). 3) Hunt: check for a preceding CVE-2025-40948 xz file read and a following CVE-2025-40949 root crontab write on the same device to confirm full-chain execution; capture any commands spawned as root.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "feature" and SyslogMessage has "key"
| where SyslogMessage contains "$(" or SyslogMessage contains "&&" or SyslogMessage contains "`" or SyslogMessage contains ";" or SyslogMessage contains "| " or SyslogMessage contains "$IFS"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage, Facility, SeverityLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog "feature-key" (";sh" OR "&&" OR "|sh" OR "|bash" OR "$IFS" OR "; /")
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*feature*key*" OR Web.uri_path="*featurekey*" OR Web.uri_path="*feature-key*") (Web.uri_query="*;*" OR Web.uri_query="*$(*" OR Web.uri_query="*|*" OR Web.uri_query="*&&*" OR Web.uri_query="*%3B*" OR Web.uri_query="*%24%28*" OR Web.uri_query="*%60*" OR Web.url="*%3B*" OR Web.url="*%24%28*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.uri_query Web.http_user_agent Web.http_method | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*feature*key*" OR Web.uri_path="*featurekey*" OR Web.uri_path="*feature-key*") (Web.uri_query="*;*" OR Web.uri_query="*$(*" OR Web.uri_query="*|*" OR Web.uri_query="*&&*" OR Web.uri_query="*%3B*" OR Web.uri_query="*%24%28*" OR Web.uri_query="*%60*" OR Web.url="*%3B*" OR Web.url="*%24%28*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.uri_query Web.http_user_agent Web.http_method | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Siemens ROX II root cron persistence via web task scheduler (CVE-2025-40949) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts CVE-2025-40949: an authenticated attacker abuses the ROX II web management task scheduler to inject commands into the root crontab, establishing reboot-surviving persistence. Article-specific: new root cron entries executing network-fetch or /tmp payloads are the persistence stage of the chain. Rationale: Maps to the CVE-2025-40949 mechanic — injected commands in the root cron table via the web scheduler. Cron parentage plus a remote-fetch/shell payload is high-fidelity: legitimate ROX II cron jobs do not curl/wget from /tmp or spawn reverse shells. Corroborated via NVD and CISA ICSA-26-134-02. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate scheduled maintenance job that uses curl/wget to pull an update from an internal server
  • Vendor diagnostic cron task writing to /tmp
  • Admin-created backup cron entry piping data out via a shell
  • Config-management agent (e.g. an internal orchestration script) launched from cron
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("/opt/siemens/","internal-update") and RemoteHostAllowlisted == true)
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the current root crontab and the ROX II task-scheduler audit entry — confirm the offending job was created via the web scheduler and points at an external host or /tmp payload. 2) Contain: remove the malicious cron entry, kill any spawned payload process, isolate the switch's mgmt plane, and upgrade to firmware V2.17.1. 3) Hunt: correlate backward to the CVE-2025-40947 feature-key injection and CVE-2025-40948 xz disclosure on the same device, and sweep other ROX II switches for identical cron entries or callback destinations.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility =~ "cron" or ProcessName has_any ("crontab","crond","CRON")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("wget","curl","/tmp/","bash -i","/dev/tcp/","base64 -d","nc ") or SyslogMessage contains "$("
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, Facility, SyslogMessage, SeverityLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Siemens ROX II Root Cron Persistence via Web Task Scheduler (CVE-2025-40949)
id: b7c9e3a1-2d64-4f18-a0e5-6c7b9d2f4a10
description: Detects cron-launched processes fetching remote payloads or executing shells, consistent with the CVE-2025-40949 root crontab injection stage on Siemens Ruggedcom ROX II.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/siemens-rox-ii-zero-day-vulnerabilities/
  - https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/17
tags:
  - attack.t1053.003
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/cron'
      - '/crond'
  selection_payload:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'wget'
      - 'curl'
      - '/tmp/'
      - 'bash -i'
      - '/dev/tcp/'
      - 'base64 -d'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_payload
level: high
source:linux.syslog ("crontab" OR "crond" OR "CRON") ("wget" OR "curl" OR "/tmp/" OR ";sh" OR "|bash" OR "/dev/tcp/" OR "base64 -d")
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name=cron OR Processes.parent_process_name=crond OR Processes.parent_process_name=CRON) (Processes.process="*wget*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/*" OR Processes.process="*bash -i*" OR Processes.process="*nc *" OR Processes.process="*/dev/tcp/*" OR Processes.process="*base64 -d*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name=cron OR Processes.parent_process_name=crond OR Processes.parent_process_name=CRON) (Processes.process="*wget*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/*" OR Processes.process="*bash -i*" OR Processes.process="*nc *" OR Processes.process="*/dev/tcp/*" OR Processes.process="*base64 -d*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Siemens ROX II three-stage zero-day chain temporal correlation (CVE-2025-40948/40947/40949) AIExploitation High
Correlates the three chained ROX II exploit stages — xz file disclosure, feature-key command injection, and root cron persistence — observed on the same switch within a short window. Article-specific: alerts on the documented 'three steps to the terminal' progression rather than any single stage in isolation. Rationale: Encodes the article's core thesis — the 'three steps to the terminal' chain — by requiring ≥2 distinct documented stages (xz disclosure, feature-key injection, root cron persistence) on one ROX II switch within a 10-minute bin, which is far higher-fidelity than any single-stage alert. Datadog query surfaces the indicators; the count/window is applied at rule level. Corroborated via NVD and CISA ICSA-26-134-02. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test replaying the full chain against a lab ROX II
  • Vendor validation run of the V2.17.1 patch that exercises xz, feature-key and scheduler code paths
  • Noisy vulnerability scanner touching all three mgmt endpoints in one sweep
  • A single benign admin session that legitimately reads a config, sets a feature key, and edits a cron job in quick succession
Suppression filter
| where not (Computer has_any ("lab","test","staging") or HostIP in ("127.0.0.1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the correlated evidence set and confirm the stages are attacker-driven (sensitive-file xz read, metacharacters in feature-key, remote/tmp cron payload) rather than benign admin work; identify the switch, user and source IP. 2) Contain: isolate the switch management plane, revoke the session, remove any malicious cron entry, rotate exposed device credentials/keys, and enforce firmware V2.17.1. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP and callback destinations across all ROX II / Ruggedcom devices for identical chain activity and stage-3 persistence artifacts.
let Window = 10m;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend Stage = case(
    SyslogMessage has "xz" and SyslogMessage has_any("/etc/shadow","id_rsa","id_dsa","ssl/private",".pem",".key"), "1-disclosure",
    (SyslogMessage has "feature" and SyslogMessage has "key") and (SyslogMessage contains "$(" or SyslogMessage contains "&&" or SyslogMessage contains ";" or SyslogMessage contains "`" or SyslogMessage contains "$IFS"), "2-cmdinjection",
    (ProcessName has_any ("cron","crond","crontab") or Facility =~ "cron") and (SyslogMessage has_any("wget","curl","/tmp/","/dev/tcp/","base64 -d") or SyslogMessage contains "$("), "3-persistence",
    "")
| where isnotempty(Stage)
| summarize Stages = make_set(Stage), StageCount = dcount(Stage), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Evidence = make_list(SyslogMessage, 20) by Computer, HostIP, bin(TimeGenerated, Window)
| where StageCount >= 2   // >=2 of the 3 documented stages on one switch inside a 10m bin
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.syslog ("xz" OR "feature-key" OR "crontab") ("id_rsa" OR "shadow" OR ";sh" OR "&&" OR "wget" OR "curl" OR "/tmp/")
ENDPOINT

ACR Stealer Uses ClickFix Lures to Steal Browser Tokens and Microsoft 365 Files

The Hacker News
2026-07-17 19 use cases 8 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

ACR Stealer, an infostealer in circulation since 2024, is walking out of enterprise networks with saved browser passwords, live session tokens, PDFs, Microsoft 365 documents, and files from synced OneDrive and SharePoint folders. It gets in because someone pasted a command into a Run box and pressed Enter. Microsoft laid out two of the delivery chains on Thursday. Its Defender Experts team, the
