ClickFix Run-dialog paste writes mshta/rundll32/pushd command to Explorer RunMRU AIDelivery High
Hunts the ClickFix initial-access step where a victim pastes an attacker-supplied command into the Windows Run box; the shell records it under HKCU\...\Explorer\RunMRU. Fires when that recorded command contains the LOLBins ACR Stealer's chains use (mshta, rundll32, pushd, conhost) or a remote/UNC target. Rationale: RunMRU is the definitive fingerprint of a Run-box paste, and pairing it with the article's exact LOLBins (mshta, rundll32, pushd, conhost) plus a remote/UNC target makes it ClickFix-specific rather than generic autorun noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://isc.sans.edu/diary/33018 • https://www.lindensec.com/post/dissecting-a-live-clickfix-attack-etherhiding-webdav-abuse-and-how-asr-saves-the-day
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power users legitimately launching cmd/powershell from the Run box for admin work
  • IT scripts distributed by helpdesk telling users to paste a benign diagnostic command
  • Software vendors documenting a 'paste this into Run' install workaround
  • Automated GPO/logon scripts that seed RunMRU on imaged machines
  • Developers testing rundll32/mshta invocations locally
Suppression filter
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("\\\\","http://","https://","mshta","rundll32","pushd","conhost") and not (RegistryValueData has_any ("\\\\corp\\","\\\\dfs\\") and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe" and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("helpdesk","svc-imaging"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RegistryValueData and resolve any http/UNC target; check whether the same host then spawned mshta.exe or rundll32.exe within minutes (join DeviceProcessEvents on DeviceId). 2) Contain: if a remote HTA or WebDAV DLL load followed, isolate the host, kill mshta/rundll32/pythonw, and revoke the signed-in user's session tokens (not just password). 3) Hunt: sweep the org for the same RunMRU string and for outbound connections to the ACR campaign domains; check for the pythonw.exe/scheduled-task persistence artifacts.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has @"\Explorer\RunMRU"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("mshta","rundll32","powershell","pwsh","pushd","conhost","curl","http","\\\\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Explorer\RunMRU"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("mshta","rundll32","powershell","pwsh","pushd","conhost","curl","http","\\")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

mshta.exe fileless chain: remote HTA fetch then in-memory PowerShell with TLS-validation bypass AIExploitation High
Hunts ACR Stealer's fileless chain where the pasted command spawns mshta.exe to pull remote HTA content, whose VBScript loader fires PowerShell that disables certificate validation and runs a JPEG-carried payload in memory. Anchors on mshta.exe invoking a remote URL/.hta and flags the .NET cert-bypass strings when present. Rationale: mshta.exe fetching a remote HTA is the documented fileless entry point; the cert-bypass strings (ServicePointManager.ServerCertificateValidationCallback) are searched inside ProcessCommandLine as enrichment, not treated as schema columns, fixing the prior validation error. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://isc.sans.edu/diary/33018
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1059.001 T1027.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy internal LOB apps still delivered as HTA from an intranet URL
  • Vendor tooling that shells mshta against an internal http endpoint
  • Admin troubleshooting scripts using mshta with a local file (excluded by http/.hta filter)
  • Security-tool self-tests / atomic red team runs
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://intranet","https://intranet",".corp.local") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("iexplore.exe","explorer.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the remote URL, resolve it, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the follow-on JPEG pull from an image host; look for a PowerShell child of this mshta with the cert-bypass strings. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate mshta/powershell, and revoke the user's browser session tokens since credential theft runs in-memory. 3) Hunt: pivot on the image-host domain and on any host that resolved it; check for Chrome/Edge 'Login Data'/'Web Data' access by non-browser processes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://",".hta")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend CertBypass = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ServerCertificateValidationCallback","CheckCertificateRevocation","ServicePointManager")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, CertBypass
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("http://","https://",".hta")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend CertBypass = CommandLine has_any ("ServerCertificateValidationCallback","CheckCertificateRevocation","ServicePointManager")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, CertBypass
| order by TimeGenerated desc

rundll32.exe loading a DLL from a WebDAV/UNC share by ordinal export AIInstallation High
Hunts the disk-leaving ACR Stealer chain that runs rundll32.exe against a DLL pulled from a remote WebDAV share (GUID directory, fake extension like .google) and invoked by ordinal (,#1). Matches rundll32 with a UNC path plus an ordinal-export invocation, and the named host sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net. Rationale: rundll32 loading a DLL by ordinal from a UNC/WebDAV path is exactly Red Canary's / Microsoft's documented example command; the ordinal-export regex plus the named host sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net make this high-fidelity and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/intelligence-insights-may-2026/ • https://isc.sans.edu/diary/33018
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1570 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise software that legitimately runs a DLL from a signed internal DFS/UNC share
  • Deployment tooling (SCCM/Intune) invoking rundll32 against a network path
  • Printer/driver installers referencing UNC resources
  • Backup/AV agents loading helper DLLs from a mapped drive
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\\\corp\\","\\\\dfs.","\\\\fileserver") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe","services.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the UNC host in the command line; confirm it is external (not a corp DFS/file server) and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the WebDAV connection over 443. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the remote host at proxy/firewall, terminate rundll32, and revoke the user's tokens. 3) Hunt: search for the same GUID-directory pattern and fake extensions (.google/.ct) org-wide, plus pushd usage mounting a remote share and conhost.exe --headless wrappers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "\\\\"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i),\s*#?\d+"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend NamedHost = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net",".google,",".ct,")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, NamedHost
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe"
| where CommandLine contains "\\\\"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i),\s*#?\d+"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

conhost.exe --headless wrapping pushd/rundll32 (ClickFix console-hiding variant) AIInstallation High
Hunts the stealthiest ACR Stealer variant that wraps its WebDAV rundll32 execution in conhost.exe --headless to suppress the console window, mounting the remote share with pushd and hiding strings behind delayed environment-variable expansion. Anchors on the rare conhost --headless flag alongside pushd/rundll32/UNC content. Rationale: conhost.exe --headless is an uncommon flag that Microsoft specifically calls out as the stealthiest ACR variant's console-hiding trick; pairing it with pushd/rundll32/UNC content in the same or parent command line removes benign headless-console noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://www.cyberproof.com/blog/the-clickfix-evolution-new-variant-replaces-powershell-with-rundll32-and-webdav/
ATT&CKT1564.003 T1218.011 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows Terminal / modern console host spawning conhost with new flags during updates
  • Developer tooling invoking conhost --headless for pseudo-console (ConPTY) automation
  • CI/build agents using headless consoles
  • Terminal-emulator apps embedding conhost
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("windowsterminal.exe","wt.exe","code.exe","devenv.exe") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the parent command line and expand any delayed-expansion (%var%) strings to reveal the hidden pushd/rundll32/host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the conhost/rundll32 tree, and revoke the user's session tokens. 3) Hunt: search for pushd mounting remote shares, the WebDAV DLL-load pattern, and follow-on pythonw.exe execution from %LocalAppData%\Temp on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "conhost.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pushd","rundll32","cmd","\\\\") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pushd","rundll32","--headless")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\conhost.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--headless"
| where CommandLine has_any ("pushd","rundll32","cmd","\\\\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

pythonw.exe silently running a script from %LocalAppData%\Temp (LogiOptionsPlus lure) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the second-stage ACR loader: obfuscated PowerShell drops a ZIP into a folder under %LocalAppData%\Temp with an innocuous name (e.g. LogiOptionsPlus) and a bundled pythonw.exe launches the Python script so nothing appears on screen. Anchors on pythonw.exe running a .py from an AppData\Local\Temp path spawned by a script host. Rationale: pythonw.exe (no console) running a script out of %LocalAppData%\Temp under an innocuous folder name and spawned by PowerShell is the exact stealthy loader Microsoft describes; LogiOptionsPlus is the named decoy folder used as a strong anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://www.lindensec.com/post/dissecting-a-live-clickfix-attack-etherhiding-webdav-abuse-and-how-asr-saves-the-day
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1204.002 T1564.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Python apps that bundle pythonw and run scripts from a per-user temp/cache dir
  • Data-science tooling launching pythonw from AppData
  • Packaged Electron/Python installers unpacking to Temp on first run
  • Developer venv activity under the user profile
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","conda.exe","code.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\Programs\\Python\\","\\Anaconda3\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: locate the .py path and the parent ZIP under %LocalAppData%\Temp; confirm the parent was obfuscated PowerShell, and check whether the installer wiped prior copies (updater behavior). 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate pythonw, remove the scheduled task, and revoke tokens. 3) Hunt: look for the second Python loader making outbound connections to blockchain RPC/Web3 endpoints (EtherHiding) and for the timestomp/PS-history-clear persistence markers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pythonw.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".py","LogiOptionsPlus")
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\" or ProcessCommandLine has @"AppData\Local\Temp" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\pythonw.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any (".py","LogiOptionsPlus")
| where CommandLine has @"AppData\Local\Temp" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hidden scheduled task masquerading as a software update, created by a script host AIInstallation Medium
Hunts ACR Stealer's persistence: a hidden scheduled task posing as a software update, created not by a legitimate installer but by powershell/python/cmd. Anchors on schtasks.exe /create with update-themed task names and a script-host or pythonw parent. Rationale: The differentiator from benign updaters is the parent: legit update tasks are registered by installers/services, not by powershell/python/mshta/rundll32; combined with update-themed naming this isolates ACR's masquerading persistence. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admins scripting scheduled-task creation via PowerShell for genuine patch jobs
  • Configuration-management tools (Ansible/DSC) that create update tasks from a shell
  • Third-party updater frameworks that self-register via a wrapper script
  • Software packaging during app deployment
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Ansible","DesiredStateConfiguration","Intune") or InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-patch","svc-sccm"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the task's action (schtasks /query /tn <name> /xml) to reveal the payload path — check for pythonw/rundll32 and hidden window flags. 2) Contain: delete the task, isolate the host, terminate the payload process, and revoke user tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate with timestamp copying off notepad.exe (timestomp) and Microsoft-PowerShell/Operational history clearing on the same host, and sweep the org for identically named tasks.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update","Update","LogiOptions","OneDrive")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","pythonw.exe","python.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("update","Update","LogiOptions","OneDrive")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","pythonw.exe","python.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python loader making EtherHiding calls to blockchain RPC / Web3 node infrastructure AICommand & Control Low
Hunts the EtherHiding C2 stage where a second Python loader queries public blockchain RPC endpoints / Web3 node infrastructure to pull a payload or C2 address off a public ledger. Anchors on python/pythonw.exe reaching public Web3/RPC hosts — no attacker-controlled resolver to seize, so process-to-blockchain egress is the signal. Rationale: Microsoft explicitly names EtherHiding via a second Python loader talking to public blockchain RPC/Web3 nodes; the article gives no fixed domains, so this is scoped to python(w).exe reaching Web3/RPC hostnames and shipped as Low-confidence hunting — validate hits against the campaign process tree. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/clickfix-campaign-uses-etherhiding-and-guloader/
ATT&CKT1102 T1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate blockchain/crypto developers running Python Web3 clients (web3.py) on corporate hosts
  • Data engineers pulling on-chain data via python scripts
  • Trading/analytics tools that query public RPC nodes
  • Wallet or dApp automation on developer workstations
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\Programs\\Python\\","\\Anaconda3\\","\\venv\\") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "web3.py")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating pythonw.exe came from %LocalAppData%\Temp (not a dev venv) and correlate with the ClickFix process tree on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate python(w), and treat the user's tokens/creds as compromised (revoke, not rotate). 3) Hunt: capture the RPC hostname/contract queried, block it, and check whether the resolved payload/C2 led to browser credential-store access or M365 file collection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pythonw.exe","python.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("rpc","web3","infura","alchemy","ankr","bsc-dataseed","mainnet","binance","polygon-rpc","eth")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Dvc has_any ("") or true
| where tostring(DstHostname) has_any ("rpc","web3","infura","alchemy","ankr","bsc-dataseed","mainnet","binance","polygon-rpc")
| where SrcUsername !endswith "$"

Non-browser process touching Chrome/Edge 'Login Data' and 'Web Data' credential stores AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts ACR Stealer's credential-access step: reading Chrome/Edge Login Data and Web Data SQLite DBs and invoking DPAPI to decrypt saved passwords, cookies, and tokens. Fires when a process other than the browser itself creates/copies/accesses these exact files under the browser User Data path. Rationale: The article's verbatim code blocks name 'Login Data' and 'Web Data' as the exact SQLite DBs ACR reads before DPAPI decryption; a non-browser process touching those files under the browser User Data path is a high-fidelity credential-theft signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/intelligence-insights-may-2026/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup or endpoint-DLP agents indexing the user profile
  • Browser sync/migration utilities and password-manager importers
  • Antivirus/EDR file scanners reading the DB (usually excluded above)
  • Enterprise browser-management tooling reading profile data
  • Chrome/Edge helper processes with a renamed image
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code42service.exe","crashplanservice.exe","backup.exe","1password.exe","keepass.exe","dlpagent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the accessing process image/path and hash; confirm it is not a sanctioned backup/DLP agent and check its parent chain back to mshta/rundll32/pythonw. 2) Contain: isolate the host and IMMEDIATELY revoke the user's browser session tokens and M365 refresh tokens (passwords rotate is insufficient per Microsoft guidance). 3) Hunt: check for exfil of the copied DB and for OneDrive/SharePoint/PDF collection on the same host; force sign-out of all sessions for the affected identity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Web Data","Cookies")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data", @"\BraveSoftware\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","explorer.exe","searchindexer.exe","onedrive.exe","msmpeng.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Web Data","Cookies")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data", @"\BraveSoftware\")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","explorer.exe","onedrive.exe"))
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Browser Access to Chrome/Edge Login Data and Web Data
id: d4b1e097-8a6c-4f23-9b70-2e5c1a0f39b8
status: experimental
description: Detects a non-browser process touching Chrome/Edge Login Data or Web Data credential databases, matching ACR Stealer browser-token theft.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/acr-stealer-uses-clickfix-lures-to.html
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/17
tags:
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1539
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\Google\Chrome\User Data'
      - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data'
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\Login Data'

  filter_browser:

      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'

  condition: selection and not filter_browser
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\Login\ Data OR *\\Web\ Data OR *\\Cookies) @TargetFilename:(*\\Chrome\\User\ Data* OR *\\Edge\\User\ Data* OR *\\BraveSoftware*) -@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\explorer.exe OR *\\CHROME.EXE OR *\\MSEDGE.EXE)
#event_simpleName=/^(FileOpenInfo|FileWritten)$/ TargetFileName=/\\(Login Data|Web Data|Cookies)$/i
| regex("\\\\(Chrome|Edge|BraveSoftware)\\\\User Data", field=TargetFileName, flags="i")
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|brave|opera|explorer|onedrive)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

Endpoint beaconing to ACR Stealer ClickFix campaign payload-host / C2 domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts network connections to the corroborated ACR Stealer campaign infrastructure (payload hosts and C2), including creativecommunityinfo.art, enhanceblabber.cc, sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net and the .icu/.sale rotation set. Straight IOC match for confirmed campaign domains. Rationale: These are the campaign domains cross-confirmed between Microsoft's Campaign 2 table (creativecommunityinfo.art payload host, enhanceblabber.cc C2), Brad Duncan's SANS diary (sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net), and Red Canary (claude-desktop.gitlab.io) — direct IOC matches with negligible legitimate traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://isc.sans.edu/diary/33018 • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/intelligence-insights-may-2026/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers/sandboxes deliberately resolving the IOCs
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling pre-resolving domains for scoring
  • DNS sinkhole/telemetry appliances logging blocked lookups as 'queries'
  • Stale browser tabs re-resolving a since-seized domain
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nslookup.exe","dig.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-threatintel","soc-analyst"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and whether resolution succeeded/connected; because domains rotate, treat any hit as high-priority and pull the host's full process tree. 2) Contain: block the domains and resolved IPs at proxy/DNS/firewall, isolate the host, and revoke the user's tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot to the resolved IP for co-hosted rotation domains, and sweep for the ClickFix RunMRU / rundll32-WebDAV / pythonw markers on any host that queried these.
let iocs = dynamic(["creativecommunityinfo.art","enhanceblabber.cc","sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net","claude-desktop.gitlab.io","deep-harborio.com","auramatrixa.com","zealpraxis.com","prism-vertex.com","prism-matrixs.com","proton-network.com","fairpoint29.com","primemetricsa.com","looksta.icu","quirksturdy.icu","strainedeasily.icu","wifihot.icu","filloco.icu","raidher.icu","apigrokcloud.icu","cpppemwjewjoiwejow.sale"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (iocs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let iocs = dynamic(["creativecommunityinfo.art","enhanceblabber.cc","sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net","claude-desktop.gitlab.io","deep-harborio.com","auramatrixa.com","zealpraxis.com","prism-vertex.com","prism-matrixs.com","proton-network.com","fairpoint29.com","primemetricsa.com","looksta.icu","quirksturdy.icu","strainedeasily.icu","wifihot.icu","filloco.icu","raidher.icu","apigrokcloud.icu","cpppemwjewjoiwejow.sale"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (iocs)

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f") or SHA1 in~ ("70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f") or MD5 in~ ("70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f") or SHA1 in~ ("70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f") or MD5 in~ ("70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DoNot Team RTF remote-template injection: Word fetching external template AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the DoNot Team (APT-C-35) initial-access step where a malware-laced RTF uses remote template injection to pull a VBA macro from attacker infrastructure, causing WINWORD.EXE to make an outbound HTTP/HTTPS request to a public host on document open. Article-specific to the Bangladesh-military spear-phishing chain that ultimately drops ejtest.dll. Rationale: Word/RTF making its own outbound web request is the observable footprint of remote template injection (T1221) described in the DoNot chain; corroborated by Cyderes Howler write-up detailing geofenced remote-template fetch of the VBA macro. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyderes.com/howler-cell/tracking-donot-apt-c-35-bangladesh-military-intrusion • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1221 T1566.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate documents on a corporate DMS/SharePoint that reference an intranet template store over HTTP
  • Word add-ins or connected services (e.g. Office telemetry, linked images) calling out on open
  • Users opening web-hosted .docx via Protected View that resolves external resources
  • Mail-merge or template-management workflows that legitimately pull remote .dotm files
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("sharepoint.com","office.com","officeapps.live.com") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the RemoteUrl/RemoteIP and reputation; open the source document from the mailbox in a sandbox to confirm an external \\template\\ or http reference in document.xml.rels. 2) Contain: block the destination domain/IP at proxy, quarantine the delivering email across mailboxes by sender/subject, isolate the host if a follow-on DLL (ejtest.dll) or shellcode staging is seen. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for schtasks creating a OneDrive-named task and for rundll32/loader activity referencing ejtest.dll within 24h.

DoNot Team second-stage loader: ejtest.dll load / invocation AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the DoNot Team second-stage DLL 'ejtest.dll', a modular implant with follow-on download capability pulled live off active infrastructure by Cyderes. Fires on the named DLL being loaded into any process or referenced on a command line (e.g. rundll32/regsvr32). Rationale: 'ejtest.dll' is a discrete, named second-stage artifact confirmed by Cyderes as pulled live from DoNot infrastructure; a literal filename match is high-fidelity with near-zero legitimate collision. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyderes.com/howler-cell/tracking-donot-apt-c-35-bangladesh-military-intrusion
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign in-house or third-party product genuinely shipping a DLL coincidentally named ejtest.dll (rare)
  • Security researcher/IR analyst detonating the sample in a monitored lab
  • AV/EDR quarantine or scanning tooling referencing the path in its own command line
  • Backup/indexing agents enumerating a captured sample on an analyst workstation
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the ejtest.dll on disk and compare to Cyderes/public IOCs; identify the loading parent process and its origin (Word chain vs manual). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loader process tree, capture memory before reboot, block the DLL hash across the fleet. 3) Hunt: pivot to the host's outbound HTTPS beacons (AES/C2), OneDrive-telemetry scheduled task, and preceding WINWORD external template fetch to reconstruct the full DoNot chain.
union
( DeviceImageLoadEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "ejtest.dll"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActorProc=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Path=FolderPath, SHA256, Source="ImageLoad"),
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "ejtest.dll"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActorProc=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=ProcessCommandLine, Path=FolderPath, SHA256, Source="Process")
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "ejtest.dll"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine

DoNot Team scheduled-task persistence masquerading as OneDrive telemetry AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the DoNot Team persistence step: a DLL implant registers a scheduled task disguised as OneDrive telemetry. Fires when schtasks.exe creates a task whose name references OneDrive but the creating parent is not a legitimate OneDrive binary. Rationale: The 'OneDrive telemetry' scheduled-task lure is a named DoNot Team tradecraft detail; anchoring on schtasks /create + OneDrive with a non-OneDrive parent isolates the masquerade from genuine OneDrive updater tasks. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyderes.com/howler-cell/tracking-donot-apt-c-35-bangladesh-military-intrusion
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise deployment tooling (SCCM/Intune) creating OneDrive-related tasks via a management agent parent
  • Admin scripts re-registering OneDrive sync tasks after an image build
  • GPO/logon scripts (cmd/powershell parent) that legitimately provision OneDrive tasks
  • Third-party backup or DLP products scheduling OneDrive-labeled jobs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("Microsoft.OneDrive","OneDriveStandaloneUpdater")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full task XML (schtasks /query /tn <name> /xml) and inspect the Action — legit OneDrive tasks point to OneDrive.exe/OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe; malicious ones invoke rundll32/loader or a Public/AppData path. 2) Contain: delete the rogue task, isolate host, capture the referenced binary. 3) Hunt: correlate to ejtest.dll load, outbound HTTPS beacon, and the delivering RTF on the same host/user.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "OneDrive"

GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash local SAM hive credential extraction AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts GoSerpent's local-hash credential-dumping tool QuarksDumpLocalHash, which extracts local account password hashes from the SAM registry hive. Fires on the named tool binary or on reg.exe saving the SAM hive. Distinct from LSASS-access detections (Mimikatz), targeting the SAM path instead. Rationale: QuarksDumpLocalHash is named as GoSerpent's SAM-hive dumper by Kaspersky; matching the tool name plus the canonical 'reg save hklm\sam' technique covers renamed binaries while staying SAM-specific (not a duplicate of LSASS/Mimikatz rules). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1003.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin exporting SAM/SYSTEM hives during legitimate password-recovery or migration
  • Backup software snapshotting registry hives
  • Forensic/IR tooling collecting SAM as part of triage
  • Pentest/red-team engagements running QuarkspwDump with authorization
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","wbengine.exe","vssvc.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the acting user is not an authorized admin task; check whether SYSTEM hive was also touched (needed to decrypt SAM). 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-reset all local account passwords on that machine, capture the tool binary. 3) Hunt: look for GoSerpent/ThumbcacheService presence, Mimikatz LSASS access, and subsequent authentication to network shares using the dumped local accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName has_any ("QuarksDump","QuarkspwDump")
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName has "QuarksDump"
    or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "save" and ProcessCommandLine has @"hklm\sam")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("QuarksDump","QuarkspwDump")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "reg.exe" and CommandLine has "save" and CommandLine has @"hklm\sam")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine

GoSerpent ThumbcacheService collection: password-protected 7-Zip archiving of office documents AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts GoSerpent's ThumbcacheService file-collection behaviour: staging sensitive documents (.doc/.docx/.pdf/.xls/.xlsx) and archiving them with password-protected 7-Zip, often from C:\Users\Public\. Fires on 7-Zip 'add' with a password flag over office-document targets or the Public staging directory. Rationale: Securelist details ThumbcacheService staging collected .doc/.docx/.pdf/.xls/.xlsx into C:\Users\Public\ and archiving with password-protected 7-Zip — the '-p' flag + office-doc/Public targets is the article-specific collection fingerprint. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User manually creating a password-protected archive of documents to email
  • IT packaging document sets for transfer with 7-Zip and a password
  • Backup/archival jobs compressing user profile documents
  • Legal/e-discovery exports zipping office files with encryption
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","7zfm.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: locate the output archive and staging DB in C:\Users\Public\; determine whether the parent is a service host (ThumbcacheService) rather than an interactive user. 2) Contain: isolate host, preserve the archive and DB for scoping stolen data, block/remove the ThumbcacheService binary and service. 3) Hunt: pivot to TmcLoader/TmcPayload activity and to writes of the archive to network shares (staging for exfil).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("7z.exe","7za.exe","7zr.exe","7zg.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-p"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".doc",".docx",".pdf",".xls",".xlsx") or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Users\Public\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("7z.exe","7za.exe","7zr.exe","7zg.exe")
| where CommandLine has "-p"
| where CommandLine has_any (".doc",".docx",".pdf",".xls",".xlsx") or CommandLine has @"\Users\Public\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine

GoSerpent toolset artifacts: ThumbcacheService / TmcLoader / TmcPayload / Stowaway / McMx drop AIInstallation Medium
Hunting sweep for on-disk artifacts of the GoSerpent toolset named by Kaspersky — the ThumbcacheService DLL/service and the second-wave tools TmcLoader, TmcPayload, Stowaway, and McMx RAT. Fires on file creation or process execution matching these tool names. Broad-net hunt to surface the campaign toolkit on any endpoint. Rationale: These are the exact tool names Kaspersky attributes to the GoSerpent campaign; a filename/service-name sweep is a low-effort, campaign-specific hunt. 'ThumbcacheService' is not a legitimate Windows service, raising confidence for that term. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Generic tool names 'Stowaway'/'McMx' colliding with unrelated open-source binaries a developer downloaded
  • EDR/AV quarantine copies of these samples on analyst hosts
  • IR responders staging captured samples during investigation
  • A benign internal utility coincidentally named with 'Tmc' prefix
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\Quarantine\" and FolderPath !has @"\Windows Defender\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash each hit and compare to Kaspersky/public GoSerpent IOCs; confirm ThumbcacheService is registered as a service and where its DLL lives. 2) Contain: isolate affected hosts, stop/remove the service, block the hashes fleet-wide. 3) Hunt: sweep for the GoSerpent Base64-encoded C2 argument pattern, SOCKS5 listeners, and QuarksDumpLocalHash/Mimikatz credential activity on the same hosts.
union
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
  | where AdditionalFields has "ThumbcacheService" or FileName has "ThumbcacheService"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, Name=FileName, Path=FolderPath, Detail=AdditionalFields, Source="ServiceInstall"),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "FileCreated"
  | where FileName has_any ("ThumbcacheService","TmcLoader","TmcPayload","Stowaway","McMx")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, Name=FileName, Path=FolderPath, Detail=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="FileDrop")
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("TmcLoader","TmcPayload","Stowaway","McMx","ThumbcacheService")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine

GoSerpent staged-data exfiltration to network shared drives via TmcPayload/ThumbcacheService AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GoSerpent exfiltration step where collected/archived data is moved out through network shared drives. Fires when a named collection/exfil tool (TmcLoader, TmcPayload, ThumbcacheService, McMx, Stowaway) writes to a UNC (\\host\share) path — the article's described exfil-via-network-share behaviour. Rationale: Kaspersky states the actor exfiltrates collected data 'through network shared drives' with TmcLoader/TmcPayload after ThumbcacheService collection; anchoring the named tools writing to a UNC path targets that exfil hop specifically rather than generic SMB writes. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1041 T1039
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backup/sync agents writing to a file-server share (but not under these tool names)
  • Admin copying archives to a departmental share
  • DFS replication touching UNC paths
  • A benign tool coincidentally named with a 'Tmc'/'Stowaway' string writing to shares
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate the destination share and files written; identify whether the source host was recently seen running ThumbcacheService/7-Zip collection. 2) Contain: revoke the writing account's access to the target share, isolate the source host, snapshot the destination share for scoping. 3) Hunt: follow the share to the next hop — which other hosts read the staged archive — and check egress from that host to external C2 to complete the exfil chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("TmcLoader","TmcPayload","ThumbcacheService","McMx","Stowaway")
| where FolderPath startswith @"\\"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, ShareName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("TmcLoader","TmcPayload","ThumbcacheService","McMx","Stowaway")
| where TargetFilePath startswith @"\\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CISA Adds Exploited SharePoint RCE Zero-Day CVE-2026-58644 to KEV

The Hacker NewsBleepingComputer
2026-07-17 5 use cases 1 technique 6 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Thursday added a newly patched security flaw impacting Microsoft SharePoint Server to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to apply the fixes by July 19, 2026. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-58644 (CVSS score: 9.8), a critical deserialization

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] SharePoint ToolPane.aspx exploitation POST with forged SignOut Referer (CVE-2026-58644)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning shell/LOLBin post-RCE (CVE-2026-58644) AIInstallation High
Hunts for command interpreters and discovery LOLBins spawned as children of the SharePoint IIS worker process w3wp.exe. Successful exploitation of the CVE-2026-58644 deserialization RCE executes attacker code inside the w3wp context; a healthy SharePoint farm produces near-zero w3wp child processes, so any cmd/powershell/certutil/whoami/net child is high-signal. Rationale: w3wp.exe is the SharePoint/IIS worker; a legitimate farm virtually never spawns cmd/powershell/certutil children. CISA MAR-251132 and Microsoft's ToolShell reporting confirm this same family drops shells under w3wp — the parent+child pair is the article's RCE impact made concrete. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/14/cisa-urges-sharepoint-hardening-after-new-exploitations • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/07/22/disrupting-active-exploitation-of-on-premises-sharepoint-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/analysis-reports/ar25-218a
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint timer/health analyzer jobs invoking stsadm or PowerShell during patch installation
  • Admins running Get-SPProduct / Config Wizard (psconfig) that shells out from an app-pool context during upgrades
  • Monitoring agents (SCOM/Nagios) that execute discovery commands under IIS identity
  • Legitimate custom web parts that shell out to cmd (rare, should be baselined and allowlisted)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("psconfig","stsadm -o","SPProductVersionTimerJob") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "OWSTIMER")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full process tree for the alerting w3wp child — capture ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, and the initiating account. Compare timing to any patch/psconfig maintenance window; genuine exploitation will show ad-hoc discovery (whoami/net) with no change ticket. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the SharePoint host from the network, kill the child process, and snapshot memory. Treat the farm as compromised — do NOT reboot before capturing artifacts. 3) HUNT: Search the same host for newly written .aspx files in LAYOUTS, command lines referencing MachineKey/ValidationKey (see companion UCs), and outbound connections from w3wp. Rotate IIS machine keys AFTER artifact removal per CISA guidance.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","certutil.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","bitsadmin.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","mshta.exe","reg.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe", @"\certutil.exe", @"\whoami.exe", @"\net.exe", @"\net1.exe", @"\nltest.exe", @"\bitsadmin.exe", @"\cscript.exe", @"\wscript.exe", @"\mshta.exe", @"\reg.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SharePoint IIS Worker Process Spawning Shell or LOLBin (CVE-2026-58644)

Webshell / DLL dropped in SharePoint LAYOUTS web path (spinstall0.aspx, CVE-2026-58644) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of .aspx/.ashx/.asax/.dll files in SharePoint web-accessible directories (TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS, wss\VirtualDirectories, ISAPI) by w3wp.exe or a shell. Post-RCE the actor writes a webshell — publicly reported as spinstall0.aspx — into LAYOUTS to persist and to exfiltrate the IIS machine keys. Rationale: The SharePoint LAYOUTS/ISAPI/VirtualDirectories paths are web-reachable; a new .aspx there written by w3wp is the textbook ToolShell webshell drop. Filename spinstall0.aspx and these directories are corroborated in CISA MAR-251132 and Microsoft's ToolShell blog for this exact machine-key-theft chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/analysis-reports/ar25-218a • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/07/22/disrupting-active-exploitation-of-on-premises-sharepoint-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint cumulative update / psconfig deploying new solution (.wsp) files that stage .aspx and .dll into LAYOUTS
  • Third-party SharePoint add-in installation (msiexec/SPSolution deploy) writing signed DLLs
  • Developer publishing a custom web part to a farm during a change window
  • Antivirus quarantine-and-restore cycling files in web directories
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","psconfig.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("SolutionDeployment","install-spsolution",".wsp"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Retrieve the dropped file's SHA256 and contents; a genuine webshell will reference Request/Response, eval, or MachineKey/ValidationKey extraction. Confirm the writer was w3wp.exe with no matching solution-deploy change ticket. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, preserve the file (copy, don't delete), and block the source IP at the perimeter. Per CISA, remove intrusion artifacts BEFORE rotating machine keys. 3) HUNT: Grep IIS logs for GET/POST to the dropped filename to find operator IPs, pivot to any process reading web.config machine keys, and enumerate all farm servers for the same filename — the webshell is often deployed farm-wide.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Web Server Extensions\15\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS", @"\Web Server Extensions\16\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS", @"\inetpub\wwwroot\wss\VirtualDirectories", @"\Web Server Extensions\15\ISAPI", @"\Web Server Extensions\16\ISAPI")
| where (FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx" or FileName endswith ".asax" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName startswith "spinstall")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS", @"\wss\VirtualDirectories", @"\TEMPLATE\ISAPI")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("aspx","ashx","asax","dll") or TargetFileName startswith "spinstall"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("w3wp.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
