IIS MachineKey / ValidationKey theft under w3wp lineage (CVE-2026-58644 post-exploit) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects processes descending from the SharePoint worker w3wp.exe whose command line references IIS cryptographic secrets (MachineKey, ValidationKey, DecryptionKey, Get-SPMachineKey). CISA explicitly calls out stealing IIS machine keys as the CVE-2026-58644 post-exploitation objective, enabling forged-ViewState persistent access even after patching. Rationale: CISA names 'stealing IIS machine keys' as the specific CVE-2026-58644 post-exploitation goal; ValidationKey/DecryptionKey/MachineKey are the exact strings the spinstall0.aspx shell extracts. Anchoring the keyword match to w3wp lineage separates attacker harvesting from routine admin key rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/14/cisa-urges-sharepoint-hardening-after-new-exploitations • https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/sharepoint-toolshell-zero-day-exploited-in-the-wild-targets-enterprise-servers/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint admin manually rotating machine keys via Update-SPMachineKey / Set-SPMachineKey after the CISA advisory
  • Farm build automation that sets a consistent machineKey across web front-ends
  • Security team running validation scripts to inventory machine keys during IR
  • Config-management tooling (DSC/Ansible) templating web.config machineKey sections
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("sp_farm","svc-spadmin") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Set-SPMachineKey","Update-SPMachineKey"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the invoking account is a known SharePoint farm admin and whether an approved key-rotation/IR task explains it. Attacker activity is spawned from w3wp with no interactive admin session. 2) CONTAIN: If unexplained, treat the machine keys as compromised — isolate the host, and plan a coordinated ValidationKey/DecryptionKey rotation across ALL farm servers (after removing webshells, per CISA order of operations). 3) HUNT: Correlate with UC2 (webshell drop) and IIS logs for forged-ViewState POSTs; forged machine keys grant persistent access indistinguishable from legit traffic, so review authentication anomalies going forward.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","MachineKey","Get-SPMachineKey","MachineKeySection","System.Web.Configuration.MachineKeySection")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"

SharePoint ToolPane.aspx exploitation POST with forged SignOut Referer (CVE-2026-58644) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the network-facing exploitation signature of the CVE-2026-58644 chain in IIS access logs: an unauthenticated POST to /_layouts/*/ToolPane.aspx carrying a forged Referer of /_layouts/SignOut.aspx used to bypass authentication before the deserialization RCE. This targets the initial_access step directly on the wire. Rationale: The POST-to-ToolPane.aspx with a Referer forged to /_layouts/SignOut.aspx is the documented ToolShell auth-bypass signature CISA/Microsoft tie to this exact SharePoint machine-key-theft chain; it is a pre-auth network artifact with essentially no benign equivalent. Defender/Datadog/Falcon left empty as IIS URI+Referer telemetry is not in those data sets in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/analysis-reports/ar25-218a • https://www.anomali.com/blog/detecting-the-toolshell-sharepoint-exploit • https://www.forescout.com/blog/threat-analysis-microsoft-sharepoint-toolshell-exploits/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SharePoint page authoring that genuinely POSTs to ToolPane.aspx (Referer will NOT be SignOut.aspx, so the combined condition largely excludes this)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys) replaying the ToolShell PoC during authorized testing
  • Security team validation of the patch using the public exploit
  • Load balancer / reverse proxy rewriting Referer headers in a way that coincidentally matches (rare)
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8") and csUserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Tenable")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Record the source cIP, User-Agent, and scStatus. A 200/302 on this request indicates likely successful bypass; correlate the same cIP for follow-on GETs to newly created .aspx files. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP at the WAF/perimeter and, if a 2xx was returned, isolate the SharePoint server and treat the farm as compromised. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the source IP across all farm front-ends, then jump to UC1/UC2/UC3 to confirm w3wp child processes, webshell drops, and machine-key theft on the targeted host. Verify AMSI integration is enabled per CISA hardening.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has "/ToolPane.aspx"
| where csReferer has "/_layouts/SignOut.aspx"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csReferer, scStatus, csUserAgent, csUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New ClickLock macOS malware traps users into revealing login password

BleepingComputerMicrosoft Security Blog
2026-07-16 16 use cases 12 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

From late April 2026 to mid-June 2026, Microsoft Defender Experts observed increased ACR Stealer activity across customer environments. These campaigns are successfully using ClickFix lures to steal browser credentials, authentication tokens, and sensitive documents from enterprise environments. The post ACR Stealer: Two observed intrusion chains amid increased threat activity appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1027 T1053.005 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1190 T1195.002 T1204.004 T1218.005 T1218.011 T1539 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix Terminal one-liner pulling ClickLock payload from compromised macOS host domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New ClickLock macOS malware traps users into revealing login password
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ClickLock LaunchAgent persistence (com.authirity.plist / com.chromer.plist) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ClickLock exfiltration/C2 to Telegram Bot API and GSocket relay from non-browser process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] osascript fake macOS login-password dialog (ClickLock credential coercion) · [LLM] ClickLock coercion kill-loop terminating Finder/Dock/Activity Monitor at sub-second cadence · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
ClickFix Terminal one-liner pulling ClickLock payload from compromised macOS host domains AIDelivery High
Hunts the ClickLock initial-access step where a victim pastes an attacker-supplied Terminal command that curls/bashes a stealer payload from the compromised legitimate domains Group-IB attributed to the campaign. Article-specific because it pins on the four named hosting domains plus macOS shell download binaries. Rationale: Uses the four compromised hosting domains Group-IB named plus macOS download binaries; a shell process referencing these domains is high-fidelity delivery signal. Domains are single-source (Group-IB) so kept alongside behavioural anchors.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately cloning/curling from a domain that later gets flagged as compromised
  • Internal mirror of a package that happens to be hosted on one of these domains
  • Security researcher intentionally fetching the sample for analysis
  • Automation/CI runner on a macOS build agent fetching a dependency
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Terminal","iTerm2","osascript")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent — confirm parent is Terminal/iTerm and the URL path fetches a shell/zip payload rather than a legit asset. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the curl/bash chain, and block the four domains at proxy/DNS. Step 3 (hunt): On the same host look for follow-on osascript password dialogs, LaunchAgent writes (com.authirity.plist/com.chromer.plist), and outbound api.telegram.org connections.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl","bash","sh","zsh","nohup")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("panalobet.ph","store.grafsynergy.com","cottonbox.co.il","gsnc.eu")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","bash","sh","zsh","nohup")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("panalobet.ph","store.grafsynergy.com","cottonbox.co.il","gsnc.eu")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

osascript fake macOS login-password dialog (ClickLock credential coercion) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts ClickLock's core credential-theft primitive: osascript rendering a spoofed macOS password prompt (display dialog with a hidden-answer field) to capture the victim's system login password before Telegram exfiltration. Article-specific because Group-IB explicitly calls out osascript launching password dialogs as the detectable behaviour. Rationale: Pins on Group-IB's stated detection cue — osascript launching password dialogs — using the AppleScript 'display dialog' + 'hidden answer' construct that any credential-harvest prompt requires. Behavioural and self-contained, no IOC dependency.
ATT&CKT1056.002 T1059.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit admin tools (e.g. some VPN or backup installers) using osascript to prompt for a password
  • Corporate helpdesk scripts requesting sudo credentials via AppleScript
  • Homebrew/first-run apps requesting authorization through a dialog
  • Developer testing an AppleScript dialog
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Installer","softwareupdated","osascript_helper")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the dialog text and icon path in ProcessCommandLine — ClickLock spoofs the real username and a downloaded Apple icon; legit prompts name a specific app. Check the parent process (Terminal/unsigned binary = bad). Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, force-reset the user's macOS/login and directory password, revoke any SSO sessions. Step 3 (hunt): Look for a repeated killall loop of Finder/Dock, LaunchAgent persistence, and outbound Telegram API traffic on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "osascript"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "display dialog"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("hidden answer","password")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "osascript"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "display dialog"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hidden answer","password")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

ClickLock coercion kill-loop terminating Finder/Dock/Activity Monitor at sub-second cadence AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts ClickLock's forced-interaction loop that terminates key macOS apps (Finder, Dock, Terminal, Activity Monitor, Console, System Settings, Spotlight) every 200–210ms so only the password dialog remains on screen. Article-specific because it targets the exact app set and the high-frequency termination cadence Group-IB documented. Rationale: Targets ClickLock's exact victim-app set and the sub-second repeat cadence (200–210ms) Group-IB documented; a >20-kill-per-5-min burst against these GUI apps is not legitimate user behaviour. Threshold/temporal so no Sigma emitted.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1056.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A power user or script restarting the Dock/Finder once or twice to fix a hung UI
  • Login-hook or MDM script that killalls Dock/Finder to apply preferences
  • QA automation cycling apps rapidly on a test macOS host
  • Crash-recovery tooling relaunching frozen system apps
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and Parent !has "jamf" and Parent !has "munki"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the kill burst comes from a single non-system parent and coincides with an osascript password dialog on the same host. Step 2 (contain): Instruct the user to force-shutdown (hold power) and boot Safe Mode per Group-IB guidance; isolate the host in EDR. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate LaunchAgents in ~/Library/LaunchAgents for com.authirity/com.chromer plists and check for crontab/shell-profile persistence (GSocket).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("killall","kill","pkill")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Finder","Dock","Activity Monitor","Terminal","Console","System Settings","Spotlight","System Preferences")
| summarize KillCount = count(), Targets = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 25), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Parent = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where KillCount > 20   // 200-210ms loop yields hundreds of kills/min; 20 in 5m is far above interactive use
| order by KillCount desc

ClickLock LaunchAgent persistence (com.authirity.plist / com.chromer.plist) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the two named LaunchAgent property lists ClickLock drops to survive logout and relaunch its password-coercion modules at next login. Article-specific because both plist filenames are exact IOCs from Group-IB's report. Rationale: Both plist names (com.authirity.plist, com.chromer.plist) are exact filename IOCs from Group-IB; a FileCreated on either is unambiguous ClickLock persistence with near-zero benign overlap.
ATT&CKT1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Extremely unlikely — these are unique malware-authored bundle IDs; only a security tool restoring a quarantined sample or an analyst reproducing the sample would create them
  • Backup/restore software rehydrating a previously infected user profile
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the plist's ProgramArguments to confirm it points at a ClickLock module path; note the writing process. Step 2 (contain): Unload with launchctl, delete both plists, isolate the host, and reset the user's login password. Step 3 (hunt): Check crontab and shell rc files (.zshrc/.bash_profile) for the GSocket backdoor, and sweep the fleet for these two filenames.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName in~ ("com.authirity.plist","com.chromer.plist")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

ClickLock exfiltration/C2 to Telegram Bot API and GSocket relay from non-browser process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts ClickLock's data theft and backdoor channels: ZIP-packaged stealer output uploaded via the Telegram Bot API and the GSocket reverse-shell relay, both initiated by shell/script binaries rather than a browser or the Telegram app. Article-specific because Group-IB names Telegram Bot API exfil and GSocket relay, and the campaign's compromised domains are included. Rationale: Combines the campaign's named channels (Telegram Bot API exfil, GSocket relay, gsnc.eu) with the compromised hosting domains, gated on shell/script initiators to strip legit browser/app Telegram traffic. api.telegram.org is dual-use, hence Medium confidence and the process gate.
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1071.001 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DevOps notification script legitimately posting to api.telegram.org via curl
  • The official Telegram desktop app resolving api.telegram.org (excluded by initiator filter)
  • A sysadmin using GSocket/gs-netcat for legitimate remote support
  • Security scanner resolving the compromised domains during triage
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".zip","sendDocument","sendMessage","bot") or RemoteUrl has "gsnc.eu"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For Telegram hits, dump InitiatingProcessCommandLine — look for a bot token/chat_id and a ZIP path (stealer archive); for gsnc.eu confirm the initiator is gs-netcat/gsocket. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, block all five domains, and revoke credentials that may have been in the archive (browser logins, wallet material, FileZilla creds). Step 3 (hunt): Trace back to the osascript password prompt, the kill-loop, and LaunchAgent/crontab persistence; sweep fleet for the same DNS queries.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.telegram.org","gsnc.eu","panalobet.ph","store.grafsynergy.com","cottonbox.co.il")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Google Chrome","firefox","Safari","com.apple.WebKit.Networking","Brave Browser","Microsoft Edge","Telegram","Arc")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("curl","bash","sh","zsh","python","osascript","nohup","gs-netcat","gsocket")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery in~ ("api.telegram.org","gsnc.eu","panalobet.ph","store.grafsynergy.com","cottonbox.co.il")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      AND (Filesystem.file_name IN ("conhost.exe","pythonw.exe"))
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name,
       Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
]
``` Article-specific bespoke detection — New ClickLock macOS malware traps users into revealing login password ```
| tstats summariesonly=false count earliest(_time) AS firstTime latest(_time) AS lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name,
       Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| append [
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Exposed Pheditor admin editor (pheditor.php) reachable over HTTP AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces any web request to pheditor.php, the single-file admin editor that ships with the hardcoded default password 'admin' (CVE-2026-55579). Because there is no forced password change, any internet-reachable pheditor.php is effectively an unauthenticated RCE endpoint, so simply locating exposed instances is the highest-leverage first pivot. Rationale: Keys on the literal endpoint path pheditor.php confirmed in the advisory and in the live repo source. Defender AH has no web-access-log table so defender_kql is empty; on Apache/nginx front ends substitute CommonSecurityLog.RequestURL for W3CIISLog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php • https://osv.dev/list
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer/sysadmin using Pheditor as an intended file editor
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Nuclei) probing for pheditor.php
  • Uptime/monitoring checks hitting the admin path
  • Search-engine or asset-inventory crawlers indexing the web root
Suppression filter
| where cIP !startswith "10." and cIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host actually serves pheditor.php and whether it is internet-reachable; check the source IPs and user-agents hitting it for scanner vs. human patterns. Step 2 (contain): If exposed to untrusted networks, block the path at the WAF/reverse proxy, take the editor offline, and change the admin password off the default. Step 3 (hunt): Review UC for POST volume (spray), action=terminal requests, php spawning shells, and newly-written .php files on the same host to establish whether default creds were already used.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/pheditor.php"
| summarize Requests=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Methods=make_set(csMethod), Statuses=make_set(scStatus), UAs=make_set(csUserAgent) by cIP, sSiteName
| order by Requests desc

Repeated authentication POSTs to Pheditor (default-credential guessing / spray) AIDelivery Medium
Detects a source IP sending many POST requests to pheditor.php in a short window — the shape of default-credential guessing against an instance that ships with password 'admin' and enforces no lockout, expiry, or forced change (CVE-2026-55579). Note: Pheditor returns HTTP 200 for BOTH success and failure, so this pivots on request volume rather than status code. Rationale: Because the app returns 200 on both correct and incorrect passwords (body 'The entry password is not correct.' on failure), a status-code 401->200 rule cannot work here; volume of POSTs to the single login endpoint is the reliable brute/spray signal. Threshold is commented and tunable. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An admin repeatedly re-saving files (each POST hits pheditor.php)
  • Automated CI/CD or backup script interacting with the editor
  • A misconfigured session causing repeated re-login prompts
  • Load-balancer health checks POSTing to the app root
Suppression filter
| search NOT src IN ("127.0.0.1","::1")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the offending source IP's full request sequence; distinguish an admin doing many file saves (varied actions) from monotonic login attempts (repeated pheditor_password submissions). Step 2 (contain): Block the source IP at the WAF, force the admin password off 'admin', and invalidate active sessions. Step 3 (hunt): If any request in the burst was followed by action=terminal or upload-file activity, treat as compromise and pivot to endpoint UCs (php spawning shell / webshell writes).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/pheditor.php" and csMethod == "POST"
| summarize Attempts=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), UAs=make_set(csUserAgent) by cIP, sSiteName
| where Attempts >= 10   // 10 = single-user admin editor should see one login POST per session; 10 POSTs/hr from one IP is abnormal
| order by Attempts desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*pheditor.php*" Web.http_method=POST by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count >= 10
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*pheditor.php*" Web.http_method=POST by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count >= 10
| sort - count
Pheditor terminal RCE invocation via HTTP (action=terminal / command=) AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to pheditor.php carrying the terminal action and command parameter — the built-in terminal feature that yields immediate RCE once the default 'admin' password is used (CVE-2026-55579, and the related command-sanitization bypass CVE-2026-55578). Requires a WAF/proxy that logs query string and/or request body. Rationale: action=terminal and the command parameter are the exact terminal-feature strings confirmed from the Pheditor source. These params are POST body so detection requires WAF/proxy body or query logging; pair with the endpoint UC (php spawning shell) for confirmation where body capture is unavailable. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using the Pheditor terminal for routine server tasks
  • Internal automation invoking the terminal action
  • Security testers validating the CVE in a sanctioned pentest
  • WAF false-parsing another app's 'command=' parameter (scope by pheditor.php path mitigates)
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Extract the decoded command string from RequestContext/body and the source IP; determine if the caller is a known admin from an expected network. Step 2 (contain): If unrecognized, isolate the web host, kill live php/shell child processes, block the source IP, and rotate the admin password off default. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to endpoint telemetry for php->sh/bash execution and any newly-dropped .php files; review outbound connections from the web-server user for C2 or data staging.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where RequestURL has "pheditor.php"
| where RequestURL has "action=terminal" or RequestContext has "action=terminal" or RequestURL has "command=" or RequestContext has "command="
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestContext, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web-server/PHP process spawning a shell (Pheditor terminal RCE on host) AIExploitation High
Highest-fidelity confirmation of Pheditor terminal RCE: a PHP interpreter or web-server process (php, php-fpm, php-cgi, apache2/httpd, w3wp) spawning an interactive shell or recon binary under the web-server account. This is the on-host footprint of the action=terminal command execution described in CVE-2026-55579 / CVE-2026-55578. Rationale: A file-editor's web process spawning /bin/sh + recon commands under www-data/apache is the deterministic on-host signature of the pheditor terminal feature; parent set covers php-fpm, mod_php (apache2/httpd) and IIS FastCGI (php-cgi.exe under w3wp). Datadog covers the Windows FastCGI case; Linux auditd lacks a clean parent field. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A PHP application legitimately shelling out (image thumbnailing via ImageMagick, git hooks, cron wrappers)
  • Deployment scripts run as the web-server user
  • Monitoring agents executing whoami/uname under the app account
  • Composer/artisan style tooling invoked by php-fpm
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","gs ","ffmpeg","git ","composer"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the child process command line and full process tree; benign PHP shell-outs are narrow (e.g. convert, git), whereas RCE shows id/whoami/curl or an interactive shell. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, suspend the php-fpm/apache worker, capture volatile memory, and block any C2 IPs seen from the web account. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate .php/.phtml files written by the web process (webshell drop), review pheditor.php modification time, and correlate with inbound action=terminal requests in web/WAF logs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(php|php-fpm|php-cgi)([0-9.]+)?(\.exe)?$" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web-server/PHP process writing new PHP webshell to web root AIInstallation Medium
Detects a PHP/web-server process creating a new .php/.phtml/.phar file — the on-host result of abusing Pheditor's file-upload (action=upload-file) or file-write editor features to drop a webshell after authenticating with the default password (CVE-2026-55579). Excludes pheditor.php itself (covered separately). Rationale: Pheditor's upload-file action and file editor let an authenticated (default-cred) attacker write arbitrary files; a web process creating new executable PHP content in the web root is the classic webshell-drop signature. Self-file pheditor.php excluded to route those to the dedicated modification UC. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate deployments/CMS updates writing PHP cache or compiled templates (Twig/Blade cache) under the web user
  • Composer installing PHP packages into the web root
  • A developer legitimately using Pheditor to create new PHP files
  • Plugin/theme installers extracting .php archives
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "cache" and FolderPath !has "vendor" and FolderPath !has "storage/framework"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the newly-written file — template/cache artifacts are auto-generated and predictable, whereas a webshell contains eval/system/base64_decode/assert or request-parameter passthrough. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the file, isolate the host, and rotate the Pheditor admin password off default. Step 3 (hunt): Search web/WAF logs for subsequent GET/POST requests to the new file path, and check for php spawning shells and outbound C2 from the web account.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(php|php-fpm|php-cgi)([0-9.]+)?(\.exe)?$" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".phar" or FileName endswith ".php5"
| where FileName !~ "pheditor.php"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php" or TargetFileName endswith ".phtml" or TargetFileName endswith ".phar" or TargetFileName endswith ".php5"
| where TargetFileName !endswith "pheditor.php"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Modification of Pheditor source file (pheditor.php) — hardcoded hash tamper AIInstallation Medium
Monitors writes/renames to pheditor.php itself. The advisory notes the SHA-512 default-password hash is stored at pheditor.php:11 and the in-app password change rewrites the hash directly into the source file — so any modification is either a legitimate credential change, a hardening action, or attacker persistence editing the admin hash. Flags changes lacking a change-control ticket. Rationale: The advisory explicitly states the SHA-512 hash lives at pheditor.php:11 and the password-change feature writes the new hash back into the source file; FIM on this exact filename catches both legitimate hardening (default hash replaced) and malicious hash swaps for persistent admin access. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1554 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin changing the Pheditor password via the app (rewrites the hash by design)
  • Scheduled deployment/git pull updating the file to a patched version (2.0.6+)
  • Sysadmin manually editing the file to remove the default hash (hardening)
  • Backup/restore operations touching the web root
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process and user — an in-app change is written by php-fpm/apache, whereas an editor (vim/nano/notepad) or unexpected account is worth scrutiny; confirm against change-control records. Step 2 (contain): If unsanctioned, capture the pre-change hash from backups, restore a known-good pheditor.php, and force a fresh non-default password. Step 3 (hunt): Diff the modified file for an injected/attacker-controlled hash or added PHP, and correlate with prior action=terminal / webshell activity on the host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pheditor.php"
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, PreviousFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "pheditor.php"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EnvoyExtensionPolicy Lua with double-slash path traversal to secrets (CVE-2026-53713) AIExploitation High
Hunts EnvoyExtensionPolicy create/update whose inline Lua contains the exact double-slash bypass paths (//etc/passwd, //var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, //proc/self/environ, //certs/) that defeat the is_critical_path check in security.lua. This is the concrete exploit signature for arbitrary file read from the Envoy Gateway controller pod during Strict validation. Rationale: Uses the exact double-slash payload paths named in the advisory (//etc/passwd, //var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, //proc/self/environ, //certs/) scoped to the envoyextensionpolicies resource — legitimate Lua policies never reference these. Cross-checked GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f and the related GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/CVE-2026-22771/
ATT&CKT1190 T1212 T1083
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team submitting a sanctioned validation/PoC policy to confirm patch status
  • Automated CVE-scanner or admission-controller test harness replaying the exploit manifest
  • A Lua policy that legitimately references /certs/ (single slash) mis-typed with a double slash by an operator
  • Backup/GitOps replay re-applying an old exploit manifest already stored in the repo
Suppression filter
| where SubmitUser !in ("system:serviceaccount:security-tools:cve-scanner") and UserAgent !has "validation-harness"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full requestObject for the flagged EnvoyExtensionPolicy and identify the submitting user/SA, source IP and userAgent; confirm the Lua references the double-slash sensitive paths. 2) Contain: delete the policy, rotate the envoy-gateway controller ServiceAccount token and any TLS keys reachable from the controller pod, and revoke the submitter's RBAC to create EnvoyExtensionPolicy. 3) Hunt: check the resource status/response for leaked token or file contents (see companion UC), and review kube audit for the envoy-gateway SA being used from unexpected sources afterward.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ("//etc/passwd","//var/run/secrets","//proc/self/environ","//certs/")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), SrcIPs = tostring(User.extra)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, UserAgent, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Leaked SA token / file contents in EnvoyExtensionPolicy status (CVE-2026-53713 disclosure) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the actual secret disclosure: an envoyextensionpolicies audit record whose responseObject/status contains a JWT (service-account token), /etc/passwd content, or a PEM private key returned by the failed Strict validation. This confirms exploitation succeeded rather than just being attempted. Rationale: The related advisory confirms the SA token is 'returned in an error which will be displayed in the resource status'; eyJhbGciOi is the constant base64 prefix of a JWT header and root:x:0:0 is the invariant first line of /etc/passwd — both are high-fidelity content markers requiring RequestResponse-level audit. Cross-checked GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A policy legitimately referencing a JWT sample string in a comment (rare)
  • Audit policy not set to RequestResponse level so responseObject is empty (false negative, not FP)
  • Security testing that intentionally reproduces the disclosure in a lab cluster
  • A PEM string embedded in an unrelated but co-located config field captured in the same response
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the leaked material from responseObject — decode the JWT to identify which ServiceAccount was disclosed and its namespace/audience. 2) Contain: immediately rotate/delete that ServiceAccount token (delete the SA's token secret / bounce the pod to force projection refresh) and rotate any disclosed TLS private keys; treat the token as compromised. 3) Hunt: search kube audit for that SA's token being replayed (new sourceIPs, verbs it does not normally perform) and pivot to the companion token-reuse UC.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend RespStr = tostring(ResponseObject), StatusStr = tostring(ResponseStatus)
| where RespStr has_any ("eyJhbGciOi","root:x:0:0","BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY","BEGIN PRIVATE KEY","serviceaccount/token") or StatusStr has_any ("eyJhbGciOi","root:x:0:0")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, ResponseStatus, RespStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EnvoyExtensionPolicy Lua invoking os/io/debug file primitives AIExploitation Medium
Broader hunt for EnvoyExtensionPolicy manifests whose inline Lua calls filesystem/OS primitives (io.open, io.popen, os.getenv, os.execute, os.remove, debug.getinfo) — the building blocks any variant of this exploit needs to read the controller pod's files, catching payloads that use paths other than the four named in the advisory. Rationale: Reading a file from Lua requires io/os primitives; legitimate Envoy request-processing Lua manipulates headers/bodies and rarely touches io.open/os.execute, so their presence in a submitted policy is a strong pre-execution signal even when the payload uses a novel path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22
ATT&CKT1059 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate advanced Lua filter that reads a mounted config file via io.open
  • os.getenv used to read a benign env var for routing logic
  • Developer testing a Lua snippet copied from a tutorial that includes os.time/os.date near os.execute
  • Vendor-provided policy template that legitimately uses debug for logging
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full Lua body from requestObject and determine whether the io/os call targets sensitive paths or is benign routing logic. 2) Contain: if malicious, delete the policy and rotate controller credentials; if the cluster runs a vulnerable version, prioritise upgrade to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1. 3) Hunt: pivot to the double-slash and status-disclosure UCs for the same policy name and submitter.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ("io.open","io.popen","os.getenv","os.execute","os.remove","debug.getinfo")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, UserAgent, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anomalous EnvoyExtensionPolicy submitter / suspicious policy name AIDelivery Medium
Profiles who creates EnvoyExtensionPolicy resources to surface rare submitters, and flags policy names containing exploit markers (poc, test, bypass, exploit, passwd). Because the exploit requires an attacker to create/patch the policy via the K8s API, unusual submitters are a leading indicator. Rationale: EnvoyExtensionPolicy objects are normally authored by a small, stable set of platform/GitOps identities; the summarize-by-submitter surfaces rare creators without a hard-coded allowlist, and the name markers catch dropped PoC manifests. Grouping/rarity is evaluated at rule level for Datadog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate GitOps controller (ArgoCD/Flux SA) creating policies — high count, benign
  • A developer genuinely naming a policy 'canary-test' or 'lua-test'
  • First-time onboarding of a new platform engineer who legitimately creates a policy
  • CI pipeline SA applying policies from a new namespace
Suppression filter
| where SubmitUser !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:" and SubmitUser !startswith "system:serviceaccount:flux-system:"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for any rare submitter or exploit-marker name, retrieve the policy body and check for Lua io/os calls or double-slash paths. 2) Contain: if the submitter is unexpected, revoke their create/patch RBAC on envoyextensionpolicies and delete the policy. 3) Hunt: correlate the submitter identity across other CRDs and namespaces for further unauthorized changes.

| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
